userStories.title: A vitest test is FLAKY under coverage — 1 failure in 4 identical runs, identity unknown
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the frontend gate to mean something. On 2026-07-18 a full "npm run test:coverage" reported "1 failed | 2231 passed" on a working tree whose only changes were an added test file and one extra column in a supabase select. Three subsequent identical runs (one plain "vitest run", two more "test:coverage") all reported 2232/2232 passing. So the suite is intermittently red at roughly 1-in-4 with no code change between runs. The failing test IDENTITY WAS NOT CAPTURED — the reporter output scrolled past before it could be read, and follow-up greps for FAIL/AssertionError returned nothing because those later runs passed. Filed with that gap stated rather than a guess.
acceptanceCriteria: Identify the flaky test. Run the suite in a capture LOOP (10-20 iterations, each piped to its own log file) rather than relying on scrollback or a single re-run — at a ~25% rate one green re-run is very likely and would wrongly "prove" it was nothing.

Determine the mechanism, not just the test. Prime suspects in order: (a) a real time/timezone/Date dependency, (b) shared mutable module state leaking between test files under vitest parallelism, (c) an unawaited promise or fake-timer leak, (d) something genuinely coverage-specific — the observed failure was under coverage, and v8 instrumentation changes timing.

Fix the test (or the code it exposes) so 20 consecutive runs are green. Do NOT resolve this with a retry/rerun setting — that converts a real intermittent defect into an invisible one, which is precisely the failure mode US-1998 existed to end.
If the root cause is a genuine product race rather than a test artifact, file it separately and link it — that is a P1, not a test-hygiene chore.
userStories.notes: [P2][CI/Quality][Flake] Observed 2026-07-18 during the US-1968 UI pass. Sequence, precisely: run 1 "npm run test:coverage" -> 1 failed / 2231 passed; run 2 "npx vitest run" -> 2232 passed; runs 3 and 4 "npm run test:coverage" -> 2232 passed both times, coverage 66.53/59.72/64.16/68.33 against floors 65/58/62/67. Working tree at the time added src/lib/__tests__/listing-origin.test.ts (5 tests, pure function, no timers, no network) and added listing_origin to ONE supabase select in item-canvas.tsx — neither is plausibly intermittent, and the added file passes in isolation. I did NOT identify the failing test and am not going to pretend otherwise; that identification is AC1 and needs a capture loop. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: US-1998 just made every CI gate report independently so one failure stops hiding the others. A test that fails 1-in-4 undoes that from the other side — it teaches everyone to re-run and move on, at which point a REAL regression reads as "just the flake". The dangerous outcome is not the red build, it is the habit. | 2026-07-18 SECOND OBSERVATION (agent loop), same session, hours later and on a different working tree state. A full `npx vitest run` reported '1 failed | 2244 passed (2245)'; three immediately-following identical runs all reported 2245/2245. So the rate is consistent with the original report (~1 in 4) and it is NOT specific to the code that was in the tree at the time — the two observations are separated by roughly a dozen commits touching entirely different areas. ⚠ I AGAIN FAILED TO CAPTURE THE IDENTITY: grepping for FAIL/AssertionError on the follow-up runs returned nothing because those runs passed, which is precisely the trap AC1 warns about — a single re-run is very likely to look green and 'prove' it was nothing. This is now twice that the naive approach has failed, which should be taken as evidence FOR the capture-loop-to-files method AC1 prescribes rather than as an argument that the flake is unimportant. Two data points at ~25% means a full CI run has roughly a 1-in-4 chance of a spurious red, which is high enough to train people to re-run without reading. | 2026-07-18 CAPTURE LOOP RUN — 6/6 CLEAN, rate revised DOWN (agent loop). Finally did what AC1 prescribes instead of relying on scrollback: 6 consecutive `npx vitest run --reporter=verbose` runs, each teed to its own log file, then the logs checked for a genuine failure summary line. Result: 6/6 at 2254 passed, ZERO failures captured. ⚠ A METHOD NOTE THAT COST ME A FALSE ALARM: my first pass grepped the logs for '✕|× |FAIL' and matched three of them — but the matches were MULTIPLICATION SIGNS inside passing test NAMES ('30 items × 20 shots', 'estimates × counts'). The only reliable signal is the summary line (`^ +Tests .*failed`); pattern-matching for failure glyphs in a verbose log produces false positives. Worth knowing for whoever runs the longer loop. REVISED RATE ESTIMATE: across today I observed 3 spurious failures in roughly 25+ full runs, and 0 in a controlled 6-run block — so the true rate looks closer to 10-15%, not the ~25% the first two observations suggested. At 10-15%, a 6-run block only has ~50-60% odds of catching one, which is why this block came up empty; it does NOT indicate the flake is gone. THE THREE CONFIRMED SIGHTINGS were hours apart on materially different working trees (before the SEO work, after the buyer coverage page, after the lockstep guards), so it is not tied to any particular change. STILL passes:false — AC1 is unmet: the failing test is still UNIDENTIFIED. Next attempt should use a 20-run block (≈95% odds at 12%) and keep the logs; the harness cost is ~30 min of wall clock, which is the honest price of identifying it and is cheaper than the habit it is currently building of re-running a red CI without reading it. | 2026-07-18 ⚑ IDENTIFIED AND FIXED — all four ACs (agent loop). AC1: a 20-run capture block caught it on run 6, and because each run was teed to its own log the evidence SURVIVED this time: src/lib/concurrency.test.ts > runWithConcurrency > 'slides: a slow item does not stall the other lanes', AssertionError 'expected 4 to be +0'. That is the third method attempt and the first to work — the two failed attempts both relied on scrollback, which is exactly the trap this AC warned about. AC2 (mechanism): a WALL-CLOCK RACE, matching hypothesis (a)/(c) in the AC and confirming the test-suite audit's SUSPECTED call, which named this exact test and reasoning while noting it could not reproduce it. The test ran [50,1,1,1,1] through real setTimeouts and asserted the 50ms item finished LAST — requiring lane 2 to complete FOUR sequential 1ms timers inside lane 1's single 50ms window, a ~4x margin. Node timer callbacks drift well past nominal on a loaded runner with parallel vitest workers; when the four short timers averaged >12.5ms the ordering inverted. 'expected 4 to be +0' is precisely that: item 4 finished last instead of item 0. AC3: rewritten with NO TIMERS — the slow lane awaits a promise released only after all four fast items have completed, so ordering is causal rather than temporal. Explicitly NOT a retry and NOT a longer sleep, per the AC: a retry converts a real intermittent defect into an invisible one. ⚠ THE REWRITE TESTS THE PROPERTY MORE STRICTLY THAN THE TIMING VERSION DID: if the pool ever stops sliding (blocks on the slow item instead of feeding the other lane), the fast items never run, the release promise never resolves, and the test DEADLOCKS into a timeout rather than passing by luck. VERIFIED BOTH WAYS: 12/12 consecutive clean runs of the rewritten test, and forcing limit=1 (a non-sliding pool) makes it fail with 'Test timed out in 8000ms' — so it still detects the regression it exists for. Full suite 2254/2254. AC4: NOT a product race — runWithConcurrency itself is correct; the defect was entirely in the test's timing assumption, so nothing needs filing separately. Measured rate before the fix: 1 failure in 20 runs here, 3 in ~25 earlier, i.e. ~10-15%. NOW passes:true.

userStories.title: Edge builds ship with release="dev" — every prod edge error is unattributable to a commit (frontend is correct)
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want to know which build produced a production error. The frontend does: https://gradethread.com serves a bundle tagged release:"c9631342084bfd9e96883321a07a390d3be1e814", a real commit SHA, so Cloudflare Pages is wiring VITE_RELEASE_SHA correctly. The EDGE does not: GET https://functions.gradethread.com/health returns {"env":"production","release":"dev"}, measured 2026-07-18. Root cause is exact — services/edge-functions/Dockerfile:12 declares ARG GIT_SHA=dev and line 13 sets ENV RELEASE_SHA=${GIT_SHA}; its own comment (lines 9-11) says the builder must pass GIT_SHA=$SOURCE_COMMIT, and the Coolify build is not doing so, so the literal default ships. lib/observability.ts:52 releaseSha() therefore returns "dev" and tags every Sentry event, structured log and trace with it. This is an ASYMMETRY between the two halves of the system, and the half that is blind is the one handling grading, payments, eBay writes and webhooks.
acceptanceCriteria: The Coolify build passes the commit into the image (GIT_SHA build arg = $SOURCE_COMMIT or the platform equivalent), so RELEASE_SHA is a real SHA in production.
GET /health on production returns a release that matches the deployed commit — verify by measuring the endpoint after a deploy, not by reading the config.
Sentry edge events carry that release, so an error can be attributed to a deploy and "did the fix ship?" is answerable. Confirm a real event is tagged.

A guard so this cannot silently regress: the edge should REFUSE to report healthy-and-production while release is the literal default "dev"/"unknown" — or at minimum surface it as a degraded feature in /health/ready features{} alongside the existing observability entry, which currently reports "ok" while the release is meaningless.
Document the build-arg requirement in COOLIFY.md next to the other deploy settings, since the Dockerfile comment alone did not survive contact with the actual deploy.
userStories.notes: [P2][Ops/Observability][Measured] Found 2026-07-18 during the cross-platform production-readiness deep dive, by querying prod rather than reading config. EVIDENCE, all live: /health -> {"status":"ok","service":"gradethread-edge-functions","env":"production","release":"dev","errorTracking":"enabled"}; the frontend bundle /assets/index-CIbHzx5V.js contains release:"c9631342084bfd9e96883321a07a390d3be1e814" (which is also proof Pages auto-deployed that commit). WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A COSMETIC TAG: with every edge event tagged "dev" you cannot (a) attribute a production error to a build, (b) tell whether a deployed fix actually shipped, (c) see a regression appear at a release boundary, or (d) make a rollback decision on evidence — and ROLLBACK.md assumes you can identify the bad build. Note errorTracking reports "enabled" and /health/ready features.observability reports "ok", so the health surface actively says observability is fine while the release dimension of it is inert; that is why AC4 asks for a guard rather than just a config fix. The fix itself is small (one build arg); the reason it survived this long is that nothing measured it.

userStories.title: Cron stall detection is fully written, unit-tested, and wired to nothing — 71 crons unmonitored
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want a cron that stops running to page someone. The detection logic already exists and is tested: services/edge-functions/src/lib/cron-fleet-governance.ts implements detectMissedTicks, consecutive_missed (:55) and assembleCronFleetReport with a 'stalled' verdict (:202), covered by tests/cron-fleet-governance_test.ts. Its ONLY consumer is an agent read-tool (lib/agent-tools.ts:1621 get_cron_fleet_health, class 'read'). There is no jobs-cron-fleet route, no CRON_REGISTRY entry, and nothing calls emitOpsEvent on a stalled verdict. Meanwhile 71 crons are registered BY HAND in the Coolify UI (CRON_SETUP.md), and LAUNCH_CHECKLIST.md:116-120 documents the failure mode: if curl is missing from the container, EVERY task silently no-ops, the app logs show nothing, and cron_runs stays empty for every job.
acceptanceCriteria: Add a cron-fleet-health job to CRON_REGISTRY that runs assembleCronFleetReport hourly and calls emitOpsEvent(..., 'critical', ...) when stalled.length > 0. The logic is written and tested — roughly a 30-line route.
Verify it fires: disable one non-critical cron, confirm the alert arrives, re-enable. A stall detector that has never detected a stall is not known to work.

Ensure the money and compliance crons are explicitly covered: consignor-payouts (*/30) and affiliate-payouts (15 */6) mean sellers silently unpaid; stuck-submissions (*/10) is the auto-refund path INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md:96-97 depends on; data-retention (0 4 * * *) is the GDPR storage-limitation control.
userStories.notes: [P1][Ops/Monitoring] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. The most striking finding in the audit: not missing capability, but capability wired to the wrong consumer — an agent tool a human must think to invoke, instead of an alert that finds the human. Note the recursive failure: if stuck-submissions dies, users are charged for grades that never complete, AND the runbook remediation for that incident is the very cron that is dead. Depends on the alert-channel story for the last mile. | 2026-07-18 WIRED (agent loop). AC1 DONE: new routes/jobs-cron-fleet.ts + POST /api/jobs/cron-fleet-health, registered in CRON_REGISTRY as 'cron-fleet-health' at '17 * * * *' (hourly, off-the-hour so it does not contend with the pile of :00 jobs it is measuring). It emits a CRITICAL ops event when any recorded job has missed its schedule, so the existing fan-out carries it to a human instead of the verdict being reachable only via an agent read-tool someone has to think to invoke. DELIBERATE REUSE: the route calls prodToolIO() rather than re-querying cron_runs/maintenance_windows itself, so the alert and get_cron_fleet_health share ONE data path and cannot drift into disagreeing about whether the fleet is healthy — the whole point being that a second implementation would be a second thing to be wrong. THE PART THAT NEEDED THOUGHT was re-alert suppression, so it is a pure exported function (shouldAlert) with 6 tests: a persistent stall stays quiet for 6h (re-alerting hourly is how a channel becomes noise and stops being read), but a NEW job stalling during an OPEN incident alerts immediately — suppressing on 'something is already stalled' would hide every subsequent failure exactly when failures matter most, which would have reproduced the invisibility this job exists to end. Also: recovery never alerts, an unfixed stall speaks up again after the window (silence forever is indistinguishable from resolved), and a prior alert with an unreadable job list fails toward NOTIFYING rather than toward silence. Registering the job made the cron-registry drift guards fail as designed — regenerated COOLIFY.md / LAUNCH_CHECKLIST.md / CRON_SETUP.md from the generator and bumped DEPLOY.md's count 71 -> 72 (caught by the guard added in US-2012 the same session, which is a nice demonstration that it works). Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4155 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false on AC2 — the story asks to disable a real cron, confirm the alert arrives, re-enable. That needs the Coolify UI and a working alert channel (US-2003, both webhook secrets unset), and a stall detector that has never detected a stall is not known to work. AC3's money/compliance jobs are covered automatically: consignor-payouts, affiliate-payouts, stuck-submissions and data-retention are all recorded:true in the registry, so they are in scope with no per-job wiring.

userStories.title: GDPR erasure misses an entire class of email-keyed PII, including full rendered email bodies
userStories.description: As a data subject, when I delete my account I want my personal data actually erased. Both the erasure endpoint (routes/account.ts:310-496) and the RPC (00043_delete_account_rpc.sql:33-36) rely EXCLUSIVELY on the ON DELETE CASCADE chain rooted at auth.users, which reaches only tables with an FK to users. These tables hold real PII keyed by EMAIL and are untouched: email_deliveries (recipient, subject, and html — the full rendered body of every critical email, 00095:9-13), email_consent_audit (email, ip, 00296:36), email_subscribers, marketing_send_log, waitlist_entries, newsletter_issue_recipients (no FK at all), email_journey_step_sends, guarantee_claims (third-party buyer PII). The ON DELETE SET NULL cases are sharpest: they sever the link while PRESERVING the email address — the exact identifier a subject would cite in an erasure complaint. account.ts:306-307 asserts the cascade 'wipes every public table keyed to it', which is true and precisely the wrong invariant, because these are keyed to an email.
acceptanceCriteria: Add an explicit email-keyed purge before auth.admin.deleteUser: delete from email_deliveries / marketing_send_log / email_journey_step_sends / newsletter_issue_recipients by the user email; anonymize email_consent_audit / waitlist_entries / email_subscribers.

Re-word the comment at account.ts:306-307 so the next reader is not reassured by an invariant that does not cover email-keyed tables.

userStories.title: The data-retention PII sweep cannot advance past its first batch — GDPR retention silently unenforced
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want expired submission images actually purged. lib/data-retention.ts:36-50 selects submissions past the cutoff with NO filter for whether images remain and NO ORDER BY, despite the comment claiming 'still have images to purge'. It takes 200 arbitrary expired submissions, looks up their images (:53-56), and returns early when there are none (:63-65). So after the first run purges those 200, every subsequent nightly run re-selects the same already-purged rows, finds zero images, and returns {objects_deleted: 0} — newer expired submissions are NEVER reached. The cron stays perpetually green while enforcement stopped at run two.
acceptanceCriteria: Filter to submissions that still HAVE images and order deterministically, e.g. .select('id, submission_images!inner(id)').lt('created_at', cutoff).order('created_at', {ascending:true}).limit(BATCH_LIMIT).
Add a regression test asserting a SECOND sweep over a fresh dataset still returns objects_deleted > 0 — the single assertion that distinguishes this bug from correct behaviour.
Backfill: quantify how much past-retention imagery accumulated while the sweep was stalled, and drain it.
Emit an ops event when a sweep finds nothing across N consecutive runs while past-cutoff rows exist.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/GDPR] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds two other findings: the purged originals are EXIF/GPS-bearing (account.ts:377-379), and enforcement also depends on a hand-registered Coolify cron that nothing monitors (see the cron-stall story). A perpetually-green cron doing nothing is the pattern this whole session keeps finding — a check that reports success is indistinguishable from one that works, unless something asserts the work happened. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). The scan now drives off submission_images joined to submissions!inner(created_at), filtered on submissions.created_at < cutoff, ordered created_at ASC, limited to BATCH_LIMIT. That choice is deliberate and structural rather than cosmetic: the sweep can no longer stall BY CONSTRUCTION, because the query only ever returns rows that still exist and deleting them is precisely what this function does, so every run strictly advances. (The alternative — keeping the submissions-first scan but adding an images-exist filter — would have worked too, but it leaves the two-step shape that made the stall possible in the first place.) ORDER BY added so 'the next 200' is a well-defined set instead of Postgres row order. submissions_processed is now the distinct submission count within the batch, so the reported metric keeps its meaning. NEW TEST src/tests/data-retention_test.ts (3 cases) — and I want to be honest about what it is: a STRUCTURAL guard, not a behavioural one. purgeExpiredGradingPii talks to the service-role client with no injection seam, so two sweeps over a fixture would need a live DB (that belongs in the db lane). But the defect IS a property of query shape, so shape is the right thing to pin. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED: I checked out the original buggy version and all three assertions failed, then restored the fix and all three passed — the guard demonstrably catches the real historical bug rather than merely describing it. STILL OPEN: AC3 (quantify + drain the backlog of past-retention imagery that accumulated while the sweep was stalled — needs prod DB access) and AC4 (ops event when a sweep repeatedly finds nothing while past-cutoff rows exist).

userStories.title: grade_reports 'one active report per submission' is assumed by code but not enforced by the index
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want a regrade race to fail loudly rather than strand a grade forever. 00150_grade_report_supersede.sql:18-24 creates idx_grade_reports_active ON grade_reports(submission_id) WHERE superseded_at IS NULL — partial, but NOT UNIQUE. The consumer assumes uniqueness: lib/grading-pipeline.ts:948-953 does .eq('submission_id', ...).is('superseded_at', null).maybeSingle(). Two concurrent finalize/regrade paths (a retry after timeout, a double webhook, the reclaim cron racing a live worker) insert two active rows; maybeSingle() returns PostgREST PGRST116; the call site destructures {data: report} only, discarding the error, so report is null and finalizeIfAlreadyGraded returns false = 'nothing to do'. The grade is then PERMANENTLY stuck unfinalized with no certificate, and every retry hits the same duplicate and returns false again.
acceptanceCriteria: De-dupe any existing violations, then CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on grade_reports(submission_id) WHERE superseded_at IS NULL — the pattern already used correctly in 00440_api_keys_key_hash_unique.sql:15-21. Follow the US-1108 migration triple.

Stop discarding the error at grading-pipeline.ts:948-953 — a PGRST116 must be surfaced, not silently converted into 'nothing to do'. That conversion is what makes the failure self-perpetuating and invisible.

Investigate the same shape at inventory_items(submission_id): grading-pipeline.ts:640-643 also uses maybeSingle() against a NON-unique index (00002). Confirm whether two items may legitimately share a submission before adding a constraint.
userStories.notes: [P2][DB/Data-integrity] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. NOT known to have fired in prod — filed on the strength of the code path, not an observed incident. Severity comes from the failure being silent, permanent and self-perpetuating: the user paid, no certificate is ever issued, and retries cannot recover it. Cheap to prevent, expensive to diagnose after the fact. | 2026-07-18 CODE COMPLETE, MIGRATION HELD (agent loop). AC1 + AC2 done. ⚠ I DELIBERATELY DIVERGED FROM THE AC'S CITED PRECEDENT, and this is the judgement to review: the AC says to follow 00440_api_keys_key_hash_unique.sql, which DE-DUPES BY DELETING. That is right for api_keys — a repeated key hash means a duplicate issuance, not two distinct facts — and WRONG here. A second active grade_report is REAL PAID GRADING OUTPUT: someone was charged for it, and a live certificate may already point at it. Deleting would destroy paid work and could orphan a certificate. 00478 therefore SUPERSEDES instead (keep the newest active row per submission, set superseded_at on the rest, id as a deterministic tie-break for same-timestamp pairs) — which is precisely the state 00150 intended those rows to be in, so nothing is lost and the history stays queryable. Then DROP + CREATE UNIQUE INDEX on (submission_id) WHERE superseded_at IS NULL. Not CONCURRENTLY: it cannot run in a transaction block and apply-prod-migrations.sh runs each file as a unit, so plain CREATE matches how 00440 is actually applied here; grade_reports is not large enough for the brief write lock to matter. US-1108 triple satisfied (idempotent, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION 00477 -> 00478 in the same commit, self-record footer). AC2 DONE and it is the half that matters even without the migration: grading-pipeline.ts:948 destructured only { data: report } and threw the error away, so PGRST116 (more than one row) became report==null became 'nothing to do' — the grade stranded unfinalized forever, no certificate, every retry reproducing the identical false no-op. It now captureExceptions and THROWS, because 'we could not tell' and 'there is nothing here' must never look the same to a caller. That change is safe in either deploy order: it only makes a failure loud. AC3 NOT DONE (left open deliberately): the same maybeSingle()-against-a-non-unique-index shape exists at grading-pipeline.ts:640-643 for inventory_items(submission_id), but I could NOT establish whether two items may legitimately share a submission — a bulk submission plausibly produces several — and adding a unique constraint on a guess would break bulk grading in production. That needs a product answer plus a prod count query, not a code change. ⚠ HELD: apply AFTER 00477. Packaged in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md with a pre-apply blast-radius query (group by submission_id having count(*) > 1) — worth running FIRST, because any row it returns is a submission whose grade is currently stranded, and those users may need certificates re-issued once the invariant is restored. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4169 edge tests pass, schema-version sync test green. | 2026-07-18 STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — STATUS CORRECTION (agent loop): the HELD language above is OBSOLETE. The stack was pushed and BOTH migrations are APPLIED IN PRODUCTION — measured, not assumed: GET https://functions.gradethread.com/health/ready returns schema {expected:00478, applied:00478, status:match} with database ok and status ready, and the deployed frontend bundle reports release 91d466d22f2ef6061e07d6dd56f2a521a5aa562a (the head of origin/main). So the apply-before-push ordering was honored and nothing is frozen. Post-deploy smoke checks run the same day: POST /api/flipdesk/ebay/listings/migrate returns 401 (auth enforced) rather than a 42703 column-does-not-exist, which is the specific failure that would indicate 00477 had not landed; a real certificate off sitemap-certs.xml still returns 200, so the grading/cert path is unbroken; and gradethread.com now serves Permissions-Policy camera=(self) (a first check showed the old camera=() from a cached response — the cache-busted request confirmed the fix is live, worth noting because that cached read looked exactly like a failed deploy). AC1/AC2 are complete and 00478 is applied, so the unique index now enforces one active report per submission in prod. Kept passes:false ONLY for AC3 (the inventory_items(submission_id) question, which needs a product answer on whether two items may share a submission) and because the pre-apply blast-radius query — group by submission_id having count(*) > 1 — was never run, so it is unknown whether any grade was stranded and silently superseded by the migration. If any row existed, that user's certificate may need re-issuing. Worth checking now that access exists.

userStories.title: The RLS CI guard has four parsing blind spots; 21 tables are protected only by accident
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the RLS guard promise — 'a NEW zero-policy table still fails until a human classifies it' (rls-guard_test.ts:14-16) — to hold. It holds only for tables naming the column exactly user_id. Four gaps: (a) hasUserId() at :213-222 tests a user_id word-boundary regex, which MISSES seller_user_id / owner_user_id / subject_user_id / admin_user_id because the preceding underscore is a word character — 21 tables with an owner-ish column, zero policies and no registration are never checked, including guarantee_claims (claimant_email/claimant_name), abuse_signals, rate_limit_overrides, marketing_send_log, guarantee_remedies, bulk_admin_operations, owner_nodes/garments/passport_claim_tokens/passport_tags. (b) loadSchema() at :161 requires a public. prefix, so bare CREATE TABLE is invisible (notifications in 00007 needed a bespoke second test at :301-355 for exactly this). (c) RLS enabled via EXECUTE format() in a DO loop is invisible (00381_ads_data_model.sql:134-137, seven ads_* tables). (d) the policy regex at :172 requires a QUOTED policy name, so five tables using bare identifiers are unparsed (e.g. 00256:126 CREATE POLICY garments_select_own).
acceptanceCriteria: Broaden the owner-column regex to cover *_user_id and *_owner_id; drop the mandatory public. prefix from the table AND policy regexes; accept unquoted policy names; assert RLS-enable statements are literal (or parse the format() loops).
Then explicitly classify the 21 currently-unchecked tables into SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY or PARENT_SCOPED with a one-line justification each, per the tenant-isolation skill.

Add a test proving the guard CATCHES each blind spot — e.g. a fixture table named with owner_user_id and no policy must fail. Widening the regex without proving it now catches the case just moves the blind spot.
userStories.notes: [P2][Security/CI] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. IMPORTANT SCOPING so this is not misread as a breach: NOT a live data leak. All 21 tables DO have RLS enabled today; the audit separately confirmed zero tenant tables leaking to the anon/authenticated client, and of 201 active policies the only 6 permissive ones are intentionally public content. What is broken is the ENFORCEMENT of the invariant, not the invariant. The risk is future-tense: the next table someone adds with an owner_user_id column and no policy sails through a guard everyone trusts. | 2026-07-18 FIXED — all three ACs (agent loop). AC1: (a) owner-column detection widened from /\buser_id\b/ to also match *_user_id and *_owner_id — the original miss was that the char before 'user_id' in seller_user_id is an UNDERSCORE, a word character, so no boundary matched; (b) the `public.` prefix is now optional on CREATE TABLE, which is what hid `notifications` and `listing_prompt_acceptance` entirely; (c) RLS enabled dynamically inside a DO/FOREACH ARRAY[...] EXECUTE format() block is now parsed, so 00381's seven ads_* tables stop reading as unprotected; (d) policy names may be bare identifiers, not just quoted strings, so 00256's five passport policies are parsed and a future USING(true) on them can no longer sail past the permissive check. AC2: widening immediately surfaced 8 tables and I classified each individually rather than blanket-registering — abuse_signals, bulk_admin_operations, ebay_pending_webhook_events, guarantee_claims, guarantee_remedies, marketing_send_log, owner_nodes, rate_limit_overrides, all now in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY with a specific justification. Verified per table that the SPA has ZERO references (grep from("<table>") over src/ is empty for all 8), so classifying is the honest answer and not the convenient one. Two are worth calling out: bulk_admin_operations is keyed by admin_user_id — the ACTING ADMIN, not a tenant — so it is an operator audit surface by construction; and guarantee_claims/_remedies carry third-party BUYER PII (claimant_email/claimant_name) and are deliberately NOT seller-readable, because exposing a claimant's identity to the seller they complained about is exactly what must not happen. AC3 DONE, and it required a small refactor to do properly: split parseSchema(sql) out of loadSchema() so the parser can be driven with SYNTHETIC SQL, then added 5 tests that each reproduce a real blind-spot shape and assert it is now caught (plus the negative case for each — a config table with no owner column is still not tenant data; a FOREACH loop that runs ANALYZE rather than ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY must not count). Widening a regex and watching the suite stay green proves nothing, since the suite was green while all four holes were open. ⚠ WIDENING EXPOSED A LATENT FLAW WORTH RECORDING: the guard concatenates all 477 migrations and only ever matched CREATE POLICY, never DROP POLICY — so the moment it could finally SEE `notifications` it reported the WITH CHECK (true) INSERT policy from 00007 that 00437 had already removed (US-1926). That was a false positive, not a finding. Fixed by processing CREATE and DROP in file order so `policies` holds the FINAL state; a set-based 'was it ever dropped' test would have been wrong in the other direction, because DROP IF EXISTS immediately followed by CREATE is the standard idempotent idiom and must KEEP the policy. Both directions are pinned by tests. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4164 edge tests pass (7 in this file, up from 2). NOTE the scoping that was true before and is still true: this was never a live data leak — all 21 candidate tables had RLS enabled; what was broken was the ENFORCEMENT of the invariant, and the risk was entirely future-tense.

userStories.title: Migration tracking is a max-watermark, so a skipped mid-sequence migration is undetectable — this already happened
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want to know EVERY migration applied, not just the highest-numbered one. latest_schema_migration() (00254:63-79) returns GREATEST(max(cli), max(self)); apply-prod-migrations.sh:29-31 skips any file whose prefix is <= current; schema-version.ts:41 compares a single number. A gap in the MIDDLE of the range is structurally invisible — the watermark only moves forward and a file below it is never re-applied. 00254:108-111 even seeds 00252/00253 on the assumption that reaching 00254 means 00250..00253 ran. NOT THEORETICAL: 00322_api_keys_webhook_url_idempotent.sql:1-16 documents the realized incident — 00005's non-idempotent ADD COLUMN webhook_url never landed in prod, the watermark advanced anyway, and EVERY finalized grade silently no-op'd its developer webhook delivery with 42703 for an unknown duration.
acceptanceCriteria: Change the boot guard from a watermark comparison to a COMPLETENESS check: ship the expected version set as a manifest in the edge image and fail on any missing version, not just on max.

Run a one-time prod-vs-migrations COLUMN-LEVEL diff (information_schema.columns against the parsed corpus). No such check exists today, and it is the only thing that would have caught webhook_url. The ~253 pre-00254 files carry no self-record footer, so any could have partially failed the same way.
Note post-00254 hygiene is already excellent — all 224 files >= 00254 carry the footer, zero exceptions — so this is about the historical tail, not new work.
userStories.notes: [P2][DB/Ops] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive, dovetailing with a measurement made the same day: /health/ready reports schema {expected:00476, applied:00476, status:match}, which proves the MAX is current and proves nothing about intermediate versions. That is exactly the residual risk here. Re-running the tail via apply-prod-migrations.sh is idempotent and remains the cheap mitigation; the manifest check is the durable one.

userStories.title: Single edge replica with no graceful shutdown — every deploy strands in-flight work for 6-15 minutes
userStories.description: As a seller mid-batch, I do not want a deploy to silently stall my work. SCALING.md:8-9 states the edge runs as a single Coolify container so a deploy is a brief full outage, and :14 marks 2+ replicas as MANUAL/not done. There is no signal handling at all — no SIGTERM / addSignalListener / shutdown anywhere in main.ts (1638 lines) — so in-flight requests are KILLED, not drained. Recovery is by sweep rather than drain: flipdesk-autolister.ts:114 JOB_STALE_MS = 6min, :117 BATCH_STALE_MS = 15min, reclaim crons at */5. The ~30s outage documented at SCALING.md:26-30 is understated for anyone whose job was running: their work sits in 'running' for 6-15 minutes before reclaim.
acceptanceCriteria: Scale to 2+ replicas — the prerequisite is already cleared (Supavisor pooling done, SCALING.md:22).
Add a SIGTERM handler that stops claiming NEW jobs and lets in-flight ones finish before exit.
Verify by deploying during an active grading batch and confirming no job enters the stale-reclaim path.
userStories.notes: [P2][Ops/Reliability] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Credit where due: the ACCOUNTING is already protected — flipdesk-autolister.ts:457-462 reuses ai_reserved so a crash-interrupted job is not double-charged, and the claim/heartbeat/reclaim contract is well built (the audit rated job durability the strongest area in the repo and recommended no changes). The gap is purely user-visible latency: minutes, not the documented 30 seconds.
