userStories.title: Correlated fail-open: one DB blip removes per-user rate limiting AND the AI spend kill-switch together
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want cost controls that do not all fail at once. middleware/rate-limit.ts:185 defaults failClosed to false and :264-267 logs 'allowing request (fail-open)' on a store error. The grading endpoint does not opt in — main.ts:821 rateLimiter(... 'grade') has no failClosed, unlike main.ts:792/:795/:800 which do. Separately lib/ai-budget-gate.ts:9-12 is FAIL-OPEN on error and :36-41 caches an EMPTY killed-set for the TTL on failure. Both controls read the same Postgres, so they share a failure domain: during a Postgres degradation, per-user grading rate limits and the hard USD kill-switch disappear SIMULTANEOUSLY while Anthropic stays up and billable.
acceptanceCriteria: Add failClosed: true to the grade and flipdesk-ai limiters, or make ai-budget-gate fail CLOSED specifically for action=kill budgets.
Ensure the two controls do not share a single failure domain, or accept the correlation explicitly and document the residual exposure in dollars.
Note the argument is the CORRELATION, not fail-open as a policy — fail-open per-control is a deliberate and defensible choice; two failing together is what turns a degradation into an unbounded bill.
userStories.notes: [P2][Cost/Reliability] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Mitigating and worth stating: the ai-limiter.ts global semaphore and daily call ceiling SURVIVE a DB outage and are the real backstop — the audit rated the layered cost control correct overall. But the daily ceiling is a blunt global, not a per-tenant guard, so a single abusive or looping tenant can consume it during the window. | 2026-07-18 PARTIALLY FIXED (agent loop). Added failClosed: true to BOTH AI-spend limiters — /api/grade/* (main.ts, the DB-backed rate_limit_grade_per_min resolver) and /api/flipdesk/ai/*. Rationale recorded at both call sites: each control failing open is defensible in isolation, and I did not change that policy generally; what is not defensible is that this limiter and lib/ai-budget-gate.ts read the SAME Postgres, so a single degradation removed per-user grading limits and the hard USD kill-switch simultaneously while Anthropic stayed up and billable. Closing the two most expensive surfaces breaks the correlation where it costs the most: during a store outage a caller now gets a 429 and retries instead of an uncapped fan-out to the vision API. Verified: deno check clean, 4148 edge tests pass. STILL OPEN: AC2 — ai-budget-gate itself remains fail-open for action=kill budgets, and the deeper question of whether these two controls should share a failure domain at all is unresolved. Also unchanged and worth remembering: the ai-limiter.ts global semaphore and daily call ceiling SURVIVE a DB outage and are the real backstop, but the daily ceiling is a blunt global, so one looping tenant can still consume it inside the window.

userStories.title: 23 route groups touching multi-tenant tables have no tenant-isolation test case; /api/account is the priority
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the US-268 per-route test rule to actually hold. tenant-isolation_test.ts is strong — 118 cases making real HTTP foreign-tenant probes — but these mounts have ZERO coverage: /api/account (reaches submissions, grade_reports, inventory_items, listings, sales, item_photos, sources — it both exports AND deletes), /api/flipdesk/images, /api/flipdesk/equity, /api/flipdesk/scout, /api/flipdesk/shopify, /api/flipdesk/depop, /api/flipdesk/google, /api/guarantee, /api/drip, /api/webhooks, plus 13 /api/admin/* groups.
acceptanceCriteria: Add cases for the ordinary seller routes first: /api/account (highest — seven multi-tenant tables), then /api/flipdesk/images and /api/flipdesk/equity.
Treat the /api/admin/* groups as lower priority and document why: adminAuthMiddleware covers them at main.ts:730-731, so they are authorization-gated by design rather than tenant-gated.

ALSO from the same audit — invert the auth allowlist for /api/flipdesk/ebay. main.ts:401-543 enumerates ~90 individual paths while other modules use a /* wildcard. All 108 currently-unmatched paths were hand-verified as legitimately public or self-authenticating (OAuth callbacks, requireJobSecret crons, signature-verified webhooks, HMAC extension routes), so there is NO live gap — but adding one route to the 7600-line flipdesk-ebay.ts with a path outside the allowlist ships it UNAUTHENTICATED with no test failure. Use a /* wildcard with an explicit skip-list.
Add a rate limiter to /api/support/assistant/* (an LLM route with none) for consistency with every other AI surface.
userStories.notes: [P2][Security/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the security deep dive. CRITICAL CONTEXT so this is not misread as a breach: the audit traced all 740 .from() call sites on multi-tenant tables, taint-traced request-supplied ids into filters, and machine-diffed every mounted route against the middleware tables — and could NOT confirm a single cross-tenant data hole. Every unscoped-LOOKING query hand-verified as parent-verified (inventory_items!inner(user_id), loadListingOwned, loadReconcilePair, or a locally-minted id). The US-268 discipline is genuinely being followed. This story closes the TEST gap and inverts a default that currently makes unauthenticated exposure a silent one-line mistake. | 2026-07-18 THREE OF FOUR ACs (agent loop). AC4 DONE: /api/support/assistant/* now carries rateLimiter(20/min) — it was the only AI surface with none. Not an open faucet before (support-assistant.ts calls loadGateAndDecide before any token spend) but every other AI route is limited, and defence-in-depth belongs on the path where a loop costs money per iteration. AC1 PARTIAL, and the probe SHAPE had to change: /api/account/export and /delete take NO resource id — they act on the caller — so assertDenied is meaningless for them and there is nothing to point at tenant A. The property that a leak would actually trip is CONTAINMENT, so the new case asserts B's own export (200, must succeed) contains NONE of A's seeded ids across the seven tables it reads. Uses EXISTING required fixture ids, so it runs in CI immediately rather than waiting on a seed change. Also added an env-gated remove-bg probe (that route writes to the PUBLIC item-photos bucket, so a cross-tenant call would publish another seller's photo) — deliberately NOT added to REQUIRED_RESOURCE_IDS, because a case that hard-fails CI before the seed script provides TEST_USER_A_PHOTO_ID would simply get muted, which is worse than skipping loudly. Plus an unauthenticated-read probe on equity. ⚠ /api/account/delete is deliberately NOT probed and I want that recorded rather than looking like an oversight: the only cross-tenant shape is 'can B redirect the delete at A', and every way of asking risks destroying a fixture account if the answer is ever wrong — a test whose failure mode is data loss is not worth its signal. The route reads only c.get('userId') and accepts no target id; that is the property to preserve in review. AC2 DONE (documented: /api/admin/* is authorization-gated by adminAuthMiddleware at main.ts:730-731, so it is lower priority by design, not by neglect). AC3 — I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO WHAT THE AC ASKED, and this is the judgement call to review. The AC says invert to app.use('/api/flipdesk/ebay/*', authMiddleware) + skip-list. I first VERIFIED the premise myself rather than trusting the audit: of 81 declared eBay routes, exactly 6 fall outside the 33 allowlist patterns, and I read every one — 5 are requireJobSecret crons, 1 is the OAuth callback verified by its single-use state token. So there is NO live gap, confirming the audit independently. The inversion is probably the right end state, but it re-wires auth for 81 live routes including OAuth returns and five Coolify crons, and it CANNOT be verified from here: a wrong skip-list 401s every cron and the eBay OAuth return in production, silently, until someone tries to reconnect an account. So I shipped the property the inversion exists FOR, at zero deployment risk: ebay-auth-coverage_test.ts fails the build if any eBay route is neither auth-covered nor listed in SELF_AUTHENTICATING with its mechanism NAMED. A second test re-verifies each exemption against the handler, so an exemption that stops being true (mechanism removed) also fails — a stale exemption is a documented promise the code no longer keeps. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by injecting an unauthenticated GET /secret-seller-report: the guard names it and fails; removing it passes. The middleware inversion remains worth doing BEHIND A STAGING DEPLOY — it is not worth doing blind, and it is now safe to defer because the silent-exposure path is closed. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4169 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false: the new tenant cases only prove themselves when the tenant-isolation workflow runs with its two-tenant fixture (they skip locally by design), and AC3's inversion is deferred rather than done.

userStories.title: Android is a plumbing skeleton, but its README and 19 passing stories claim near-parity
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the Android backlog to reflect reality. Android has genuinely good infrastructure — auth, a Room sync engine, mutation queue, delete reconciliation, telemetry, app-lock, CameraX capture, ~70 Kotlin files. It has no product: every navigation destination except one is a literal placeholder (ui/shell/AppShell.kt:162-175 — Home, Inventory, Money, Marketplaces, Settings, Details intake, AutoLister all render SectionPlaceholder; only capture/photos is real). Corroborating: Android calls exactly ONE edge endpoint in the entire codebase (/api/flipdesk/photo-profiles) versus iOS's 77 and web's ~530 — no grading submit, no inventory read, no eBay, no payments. Two documentation problems compound it: android/README.md:31-39 presents a package map for grading / inventory / marketplaces / money / billing whose directories contain ZERO .kt files, and :3 calls it 'at iOS parity'. And 19 stories are marked passes:true with no implementing code — verified: US-1380 Glance widgets (zero 'glance' references anywhere, no AppWidgetProvider in the manifest), US-1378 FCM push (no FirebaseMessaging reference), US-1383 Settings (routes to a placeholder), US-1384/1385/1387/1388/1389, US-1393 localization (no values-* locale dirs). The pattern is clean: US-1300-1328 (infrastructure) are genuinely done; US-1378-1396 is a contiguous block marked done without code.
acceptanceCriteria: Re-open the falsely-passing Android stories (start with the verified list: US-1380, US-1378, US-1383, US-1384, US-1385, US-1387, US-1388, US-1389, US-1393) and audit the rest of the US-1378-1396 block the same way.
Correct android/README.md — remove the 'at iOS parity' claim and the package map for directories that contain no code. This is the first document a new engineer or a diligence reviewer reads.
Re-baseline the Android estimate: real completion is closer to 29/98 than the 48/98 the backlog implies, and ALL remaining work is the expensive UI/feature half rather than a polish pass.
Decide explicitly whether Android is on the launch plan. If it is, the remaining work is essentially the whole app.
userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Backlog-integrity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. This is the same class as US-1996 (archived stories marked passes:true that were explicitly DEFERRED) but larger and on a platform nobody is looking at. The state is more misleading than a plain stub would be: sophisticated offline-sync infrastructure attached to zero features reads as 'nearly done' to anyone who opens the project and sees the hard parts solved. NOT verified: whether the 50 OPEN Android stories are correctly open — only the passing ones were falsified.

userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it.

userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session.

userStories.title: Three fully-built marketplace OAuth connectors (Depop/Etsy/Whatnot) are live with zero callers
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we do not want live token-minting endpoints with no product behind them. 937 lines of production OAuth code have no caller on any client: routes/flipdesk-depop.ts (388 lines, /oauth/start:80, /oauth/callback:127, /oauth/refresh:216, /disconnect:226), flipdesk-etsy.ts (311 lines), flipdesk-whatnot.ts (238 lines) — web 0, iOS 0, extension 0. All three are mounted and live (main.ts:1049-1051). They are also HALF connectors: OAuth plus disconnect only, no publish/revise, so even with UI they could not list. Also uncalled by any client: /api/drip, /api/campaign-track, /api/changelog.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide per connector: gate behind a feature flag, or delete. Live authenticated endpoints that mint and store marketplace tokens are attack surface and an audit finding with zero offsetting value while unreachable.
If keeping them for a near-term launch, say so in the story and add the missing publish/revise half — an OAuth-only connector cannot deliver the feature it implies.
Re-check /api/drip, /api/campaign-track and /api/changelog the same way (note /api/drip is separately in scope for the tenant-isolation test gap).
userStories.notes: [P2][Security/Dead-code] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Related: US-1662 tracks Whatnot listing publish/update/delist as open, so the Whatnot OAuth half was likely built ahead of it — that is the benign reading. The security point stands regardless: unreachable-but-live token endpoints expand the attack surface without expanding the product, and they will be found in any diligence review.

userStories.title: 50+ documented lockstep mirrors are enforced by comments; only ONE has an automated guard
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want cross-platform contract drift to be caught by CI rather than by an incident. The repo is admirably self-aware — 50+ explicit mirror/lockstep markers exist (src/lib/constants.ts:1059-1061 'MUST stay in lockstep', autolister-verify-windows.ts:12-13, best-offer-thresholds.ts:1-6, grading-readiness.ts:6 'Client-side mirror of buildValidation()', cert-number.ts:16, grade-standard.ts:2,16, listing-origin.ts:3, garment-mapping.ts:6, constants.ts:565,1118,1440,1489). iOS adds a THIRD copy of many (AIExtract/AIExtractTypes.swift:3, AIItemFieldWriter.swift:14, Analytics/ListingPerformanceModels.swift:3,96,142, SourceROIRollup.swift:8,99). Exactly ONE has an automated guard — Class A storage, per IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:32-34 (item-photo-storage_test.ts). The edge test dir has just 4 guard tests (ads-guardrails, rls-guard, support-output-guard, us1507-relist-guard), none covering the pricing, grading-readiness or legal-version mirrors.
acceptanceCriteria: Generalize the Class A pattern: for each high-risk mirror, add a shared behavioural FIXTURE asserted by every copy's suite (the remedy US-1995 already applied to title-sync), rather than source-diffing.
Prioritize the mirrors where divergence is silent and expensive: grading-readiness (buildValidation), best-offer thresholds, pricing constants, legal versions (see the legal story), grade-standard.
IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:80-84 already names this fix ('Source-guards for contracts — cheap, deterministic') and it was never generalized beyond Class A. Close that out.
userStories.notes: [P2][Architecture/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The repo's OWN post-mortem (IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md:11-20) says all three bugs in the original cluster were exactly this class, missed because unit tests pass on both sides independently while the seam diverges. This session hit the same pattern twice more: US-1995 (edge title-sync mirror with zero callers) and the ai-size-estimate-core dead copy. A comment asserting a link is not the link. | 2026-07-18 SECOND MIRROR PINNED — grading-readiness (agent loop). Following the same shape as the weighted-grade fixture (US-2041) earlier today. The edge's readiness rules were inline inside buildValidation, so the web mirror (previewGradingReadiness) could not be compared to anything; the two were held together by a comment stating 'the blocker STRINGS below are verbatim copies of the server's'. Extracted gradingReadinessBlockers() as a PURE exported function in flipdesk-grading.ts, had buildValidation call it (no behaviour change), and added src/test/fixtures/grading-readiness-cases.json — 13 cases asserted by BOTH suites. WHY THIS MIRROR RANKED HIGH: divergence is silent in BOTH directions and both are expensive — a client saying READY when the server disagrees sends a seller into a submit-time rejection, and a client saying NOT READY when the server would accept blocks them from paying us. The fixture deliberately covers the semantic edge that the copy exists to make: a 'defect' photo does NOT satisfy the fabric close-up requirement, because the pipeline ABSTAINS without a real weave/knit shot — if that rule drifts, a seller pays for a grade that comes back ungraded. Also pinned the exact blocker STRINGS, since the web card regex-matches them (onlyGarmentBlocks), making them a cross-project contract rather than mere copy. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FROM BOTH SIDES independently: renaming 'Missing garment_type' to 'Missing garment type' in the WEB copy fails the vitest guard; deleting the fabric-close-up rule from the EDGE authority fails the deno guard. Restoring passes both. Verified: tsc clean, eslint 0 errors, 2242 vitest + 4188 deno tests pass. STILL passes:false — AC2 names five priority mirrors and two are now pinned (grade-standard/weights via US-2041, grading-readiness here). Remaining: best-offer thresholds, pricing constants, and legal versions (the last is US-2017 and is the compliance-sensitive one — clients hardcode a version the server derives from the DB). | 2026-07-18 AC2 COMPLETE — all five priority mirrors pinned (agent loop). Best-offer thresholds is the last: src/test/fixtures/best-offer-threshold-cases.json (14 cases) asserted by BOTH src/lib/__tests__/best-offer-thresholds.test.ts and services/edge-functions/src/tests/best-offer-parity_test.ts. The fixture targets the CONSTRAINT BOUNDARIES rather than happy paths, because that is where a drift changes behaviour: accept exactly AT list (nudged to one cent under), accept above list, a 1-cent listing that leaves no room for any accept, decline equal to accept, decline above accept, decline at/above list with no accept, zero and negative overrides, and fractional cents. These constraints are EBAY'S, not ours — eBay REJECTS a publish where autoAcceptPrice is not strictly below the listing price — so a drift means the composer cheerfully SAVES thresholds that fail at publish, after the seller believes they are finished. Also pinned the deliberate product behaviour that an inverted decline is DROPPED rather than silently rewritten: quietly 'fixing' a seller's number to satisfy eBay would change a figure they chose without telling them. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from both sides: removing the accept-below-list clamp from the WEB mirror fails 2 vitest assertions; removing the inverted-decline drop from the EDGE authority fails the deno guard. ⚠ TWO THINGS WORTH RECORDING. (1) The two copies' TYPES differed subtly — the edge declares all five inputs required-but-nullable — so my first fixture (omitting keys) only type-checked against the web mirror. Supplying all five explicitly removed a cast AND made the table usable by both. (2) `tsc -b` caught an incomplete input in my own new test that VITEST had passed, because vitest does not typecheck. A test suite going green is not the same as the test being well-formed. FIVE OF FIVE now pinned: grade weights + rounding (US-2041), grading-readiness, legal versions (US-2017), pricing/credit-packs (US-2075), best-offer thresholds. AC1's broader sweep of the remaining ~45 documented mirrors is still open, but the five the audit named as highest-risk are done. | 2026-07-18 AC1 + AC3 DONE — story complete (agent loop). Rather than hand-fixing the remaining ~45 mirrors (≈45 commits, and the NEXT one would still be unguarded), added src/lib/__tests__/lockstep-registry.test.ts: it DISCOVERS every file whose comments assert a lockstep relationship and forces each to be classified as PINNED (a named fixture/test asserts both copies) or EXEMPT (with a stated reason ≥60 chars, enforced). Same shape as SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY in rls-guard_test.ts — a NEW mirror fails the build by name until a human decides which it is. That converts an unbounded manual backlog into a bounded, self-maintaining one. Three sub-guards: unclassified-file detection, a STALE-ENTRY check (a registry naming files that no longer declare a mirror rots into noise and hides which entries are load-bearing), and an EXEMPT-must-justify check. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by adding a throwaway file containing 'client mirror of … keep the two in lockstep': the guard failed and named it; removing it passed. ⚠ THE CLASSIFICATION WAS DONE BY READING EACH FILE, not by pattern-matching, and the distinctions are the actual content. EXEMPT is not 'unimportant' — each entry names why a drift is RECOVERABLE: use-buyer-entitlements mirrors subscription statuses the server re-checks on every gated action; verified.ts mirrors a rule ALSO enforced by a DB CHECK (00057), so a drift yields a rejected write rather than bad data; signup.tsx's password mirror is explicitly non-authoritative and the policy itself is pinned elsewhere; autolister.tsx is an intra-file CSS value, not cross-project at all; publish-preflight mirrors something WITHIN the edge project where an ordinary import test suffices. And ebay-prefill.ts turned out to be the best-guarded of the lot — its registry is GENERATED from the edge via `npm run sync:aspects` with a CI drift guard, i.e. the data cannot be hand-edited out of sync at all, which is a stronger mechanism than any fixture. Also had to exclude the guard file from its own scan (it documents the marker phrases in order to search for them). NOW passes:true: AC1 (generalized), AC2 (all five priority mirrors pinned), AC3 (IOS_PARITY_AUDIT's 'source-guards for contracts' closed out).

userStories.title: Three browser extensions are maintained in parallel against the same marketplace DOMs
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want one extension to maintain, not three. Three separate MV3 extensions are all receiving active commits: extension (Lister, v0.1.0, last commit 2026-07-13), extension-condition (Condition Check, v0.2.1, 2026-07-15) and extension-unified ('Grade & List', v0.3.5, 2026-07-18). The name 'unified' implies it supersedes the other two, but both predecessors are still getting feature work — extension-condition received US-1884 accessibility work on 07-15.
acceptanceCriteria: Confirm whether extension and extension-condition are deprecated in favour of extension-unified. If so, freeze them and stop investing.

If all three ship, document why — three Chrome Web Store listings mean three review cycles and three selector-maintenance burdens against the same marketplace DOMs, which is the expensive part when a marketplace changes its markup.
Cross-check against US-1872 (unified extension epic) and US-1881 (Firefox/Edge support), which assume a single artifact.
userStories.notes: [P3][Extension/Maintenance] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Likely a migration in progress rather than a mistake — filed so the migration gets finished deliberately instead of leaving three live artifacts drifting apart.

userStories.title: email_deliveries stores full rendered email bodies forever with no purge
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the email log bounded. 00095_email_deliveries.sql:9-24 stores recipient, subject and 'html text not null' — the complete rendered body — for every critical send, with rows kept at status sent/dead_letter. There is NO purge anywhere: the only pruning in lib/data-retention.ts:132 is cron_runs (30-day window). No DELETE FROM email_deliveries exists in the codebase.
acceptanceCriteria: Extend the data-retention cron: delete sent rows older than ~90 days, and null out html on dead_letter rows once triaged.
Coordinate with the GDPR erasure story — this table is the single largest reservoir of un-erasable PII (it is email-keyed, so the deletion cascade never reaches it).

Note the operational cost too: one full HTML document per critical email, forever, becomes the largest table in the DB and inflates backup and restore windows — which directly worsens the RTO in the backup story.
userStories.notes: [P3][DB/Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds three other findings at once: GDPR erasure (un-erasable PII), backup/restore duration (RTO), and the stalled retention sweep (the cron that would own this purge is itself not advancing). The partial index email_deliveries_due_idx (:31-33) stays healthy while the heap does not, so query performance will not warn you. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC1 DONE, with TWO DIFFERENT RULES rather than the one the AC implied — the distinction matters and is the whole risk of this change: (1) status='sent' rows are pure history once delivered, so they are DELETED after 90 days (well past any support window that would need to re-read what a user was actually sent); (2) status='dead_letter' rows are an OPERATOR REPLAY QUEUE and are NEVER deleted — only their heavy PII-bearing `html` body is stripped, and on a longer 180-day window so a genuine replay stays possible. Deleting dead-letters would destroy the evidence that mail went UNDELIVERED, which is the entire purpose of a dead-letter table; the careless version of this fix (one unscoped DELETE) would have quietly eaten that queue while looking like a successful cleanup. Both cutoffs are named constants with the reasoning inline. Wired into the existing data-retention cron next to the cron_runs prune, and best-effort for the same stated reason — a prune hiccup must never fail the PII purge that is the job's reason to exist. THREE NEW TESTS in data-retention_test.ts, all NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by simulating the exact careless edits: removing .eq('status','sent') fails the scoping test, and switching the dead-letter .update({html:''}) to .delete() fails the body-strip test; restoring passes. Checked against the repo gotcha too — no .or() on an UPDATE/DELETE (US-1552), only .eq/.lt/.neq, so this cannot hit the self-hosted PostgREST 42703 that CI would not catch. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4167 edge tests pass. AC2 CONTEXT: this directly reduces the un-erasable-PII reservoir called out in US-2005 (email_deliveries was its single largest contributor) and shrinks the backup/restore window that worsens the RTO in US-2002 — the three findings were compounding each other. STILL passes:false on AC3's quantification: how much this actually reclaims, and how much accumulated while there was no purge at all, needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')). Worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed, and worth knowing that the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned.

userStories.title: Consignor payouts are never reversed when the sale is later returned or refunded
userStories.description: As a seller, when a consigned item comes back I must not be out the consignor's cut. lib/consignor-payout.ts:105 gates NEW payouts on sale.status === 'completed', but there is NO reversal path for one already settled. flipdesk-ebay.ts:3626 flips sales.status to returned/refunded on an eBay return or approved cancellation and restores the inventory item — and touches nothing in consignor_payouts. Once fireTransfer (consignor-payout.ts:322-335) has moved money to the consignor's Connect account and set status='paid', SETTLED_STATUSES (consignor-payout-math.ts:69) makes every later evaluation return skip('already_settled'). A repo-wide grep for 'clawback' finds it in the affiliate, Stripe-metadata, Apple and Google paths — nothing in the consignor engine.
acceptanceCriteria: On the sale-status transition to returned/refunded (flipdesk-ebay.ts:3626 and any other writer), look up consignor_payouts for the affected sale_id(s).

Cancel pending/failed rows outright; for PAID rows either issue a Stripe transfers.createReversal (idempotency-keyed on the payout id, matching the existing consignor_payout_ key convention) or write a negative-balance row that offsets the consignor's next payout. Pick one and say why in the notes.
Consider a hold window before transfer, mirroring the affiliate engine's hold_days — the cheapest fix for most of this exposure is not paying out until the return window closes.
Surface it: a paid payout on a returned sale must appear somewhere an operator sees, because today the row stays 'paid' and nothing signals the loss.
userStories.notes: [P1][Money/Consignment] Found 2026-07-18 by the money-correctness deep dive. LARGEST PER-INCIDENT DOLLAR EXPOSURE in the codebase: a $200 consigned item at a 60% split transfers $120 to the consignor; the buyer returns it 20 days later and eBay refunds them $200 from the seller. The seller eats $120 with no automated recovery and NO SIGNAL — the payout row still reads 'paid'. Note the shape: this is not a bug in the payout engine, which is well built (pre-flight transfer lookup defeats Stripe's 24h key TTL, math is separated and tested). It is a MISSING EDGE between two subsystems that each work correctly on their own. Source-only finding: the Stripe MCP connector needs authorization, so live transfer/reversal state was not checked.

userStories.title: inventory.tsx paginates the grid, then loads the tenant's ENTIRE listings + sales history anyway
userStories.description: As a seller with real volume, opening Inventory must not download my whole commercial history. src/pages/inventory.tsx:156-159 issues supabase.from('listings').select('*') and supabase.from('sales').select('*') with NO limit, range or filter — only RLS tenant scoping. The grid itself IS correctly paginated (:229 uses .range(page*PAGE_SIZE)) and counts via count:'exact' (:203). The two unbounded reads exist only to build listingsByItem / saleByItem maps (:171-182) for a days-listed column on the ~50 visible rows. Same file :135-137 fetches inventory_items.select('brand') for EVERY row in the tenant just to populate a distinct-brand filter dropdown.
acceptanceCriteria: Scope both hydration queries to the page's item ids: .in('inventory_item_id', itemRows.map(r => r.id)), selecting only the columns the column needs (inventory_item_id, listed_at / sold_at). Both supporting indexes already exist (idx_listings_inventory_item_id, idx_sales_inventory_item_id).
Replace the whole-tenant brand scan with a distinct RPC or a maintained brand list.
Verify with a seeded heavy account (thousands of rows) that the Inventory payload is bounded by page size, not by account age.
userStories.notes: [P1][Perf/Frontend] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive (the pass the ops audit flagged as owed and explicitly NOT done). Concrete scenario: a seller with 5,000 listings and 3,000 sales pulls 8,000 WIDE rows (select('*') on two wide tables; sales carries fee/payout/tracking/buyer columns) into a browser to decorate 50 grid rows. Multi-MB payload plus main-thread JSON parse on the entry path to the app, and it grows monotonically forever because sales is append-only. staleTime 5min limits refetch frequency, not the first paint of every session. Highest value-to-effort ratio in the whole performance audit — roughly an hour's work. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (main finding) (agent loop). inventory.tsx no longer loads the tenant's entire listings + sales history. The hydration query moved AFTER the paginated page query and is now scoped .in('inventory_item_id', pageItemIds) and projected to the only TWO columns calcDaysListed actually reads (listed_at, sale_date) — down from select('*') on two wide tables with no bound at all. Payload is now proportional to PAGE_SIZE instead of to account age; both supporting indexes already existed. Narrowed the helper's parameter types to DaysListedListing/DaysListedSale so widening the projection later requires widening a type — a visible decision rather than silent drift. ⚠ CAUGHT WHILE FIXING: `items` was `data?.items ?? []`, a fresh array identity every render, and my new pageItemIds memo derives from it and feeds a queryKey. TanStack hashes keys structurally so this was NOT causing refetch churn — but eslint flagged it and relying on that hashing is incidental rather than obvious, so `items` is memoized. STILL passes:false on AC2: the distinct-brand dropdown at :132-137 STILL scans every inventory_items row in the tenant to produce ~200 strings. I left it deliberately — PostgREST cannot do DISTINCT without an RPC, and the available client-side workarounds (a limit, or sampling) would silently DROP brands from the filter, which is a correctness regression traded for a perf win. It needs the RPC, which means a migration, and I did not want to stack a third held migration.

userStories.title: Bulk grading submit is an unbounded N+1 that can charge credits and then time out
userStories.description: As a seller bulk-grading, a large batch must not half-charge me. services/edge-functions/src/routes/flipdesk-grading.ts:419 loops `for (const item of validation.result.items)` and inside it (:490-494) issues a per-item item_photos SELECT — a strict regression against the validation pass in the SAME FILE, which at :193-197 already loads photo coverage for all items in ONE .in('inventory_item_id', itemIds) query with the comment 'Photo coverage — one query covering all items'. Each iteration also INSERTs a submission (:455-465), runs runPaymentPrecedence (:476, itself several queries), copies photos in storage, and inserts links — all sequential, no Promise.all. NOTHING BOUNDS THE BATCH: inputs.length is validated only for === 0 (:109) and submitBodySchema enforces no max that reaches this loop.
acceptanceCriteria: Cap the batch size at the schema, with a clear error when exceeded.
Hoist the item_photos fetch out of the loop, reusing the .in() pattern already present at :193.
Chunk the remaining per-item work with bounded concurrency rather than a fully sequential loop.

Address the partial-charge window: the loop sets charged = true at :487 BEFORE the photo copy, and the catch-block compensation handles a THROWN error, not a killed isolate. Decide what a timed-out batch owes the seller and make it recoverable.
userStories.notes: [P1][Perf/Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. This one has a correctness dimension, not just latency: 200 selected items is ~1,000+ sequential round trips plus storage copies in a single request — near-certain edge timeout — and because credits are charged per item inside the loop, a timeout leaves a PARTIALLY CHARGED batch that the compensation path does not cover (it catches thrown errors; an isolate kill throws nothing). Fixing the N+1 also shrinks the window in which that can happen, but the charge/commit ordering deserves its own thought. | 2026-07-18 N+1 FIXED, AC1 WAS ALREADY TRUE (agent loop). ⚠ CORRECTION TO THIS STORY'S OWN PREMISE, which I inherited from the audit and verified rather than trusted: AC1 says 'nothing bounds the batch' and cites submitBodySchema as enforcing no max. FALSE — flipdesk-grading.ts:305 has carried .max(200, 'a batch may contain at most 200 items') all along. The audit checked inputs.length in buildValidation (validated only for === 0) and missed the schema-level cap on the route body. So the loop was bounded at 200, not unbounded. I added a test pinning the cap so the claim cannot drift in either direction. AC2 DONE: both per-item queries hoisted. inventory_items and item_photos are now loaded ONCE for the whole batch via .in(batchItemIds) in a Promise.all before the loop, then read from maps — mirroring what buildValidation() in the same file already did correctly ('Photo coverage — one query covering all items'). That removes ~400 sequential round trips at the cap. The batch item query is also .eq('user_id', ownerId) server-side (US-268: the ids come from the request body), with the per-item ownership assertion kept as defence in depth. AC3 (bounded-concurrency chunking) NOT done: the loop still runs sequentially. It writes submissions, charges credits and copies storage objects per item, and parallelizing WRITES that charge money is not a change to make without thinking about what concurrent partial failure means — the current sequential loop at least fails in a defined order. AC4 (the partial-charge window) NOT done and is the real remaining risk: `charged = true` is set before the photo copy, and the catch-block compensation handles a THROWN error, so a killed isolate leaves a partially-charged batch nothing reverses. Removing the N+1 SHRINKS that window but does not close it; closing it needs either a reservation/commit split or a sweeper that reconciles charged-but-incomplete submissions. NEW TEST grading-submit-batch_test.ts (5 cases) pins the batching, the absence of per-item selects, the tenant scoping, the cap, AND — the subtle one — that grouping an ordered result set into a map preserves per-item sort_order, since detail_1/2/3 landing out of order would silently give the grader the wrong lead image. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4178 edge tests pass.

userStories.title: RouteErrorFallback reports nothing to Sentry — including the partner embed route
userStories.description: As GradeThread, a route-level crash must produce telemetry. The class ErrorBoundary calls captureException (src/components/error-boundary.tsx:36), but the router errorElement — RouteErrorFallback at :108-141, used at src/routes/index.tsx:354 and :765 — does not. Route errors render a 'Page Error' card with ZERO telemetry. The sharpest case is /embed/grade/:id (routes/index.tsx:762-766), which sits OUTSIDE RootLayout and therefore has no class boundary above it: a white-label partner iframe can be broken indefinitely with nobody knowing.
acceptanceCriteria: Call useRouteError() + captureException in a useEffect inside RouteErrorFallback, matching what the class boundary already does.
Confirm an embed-route error actually produces a Sentry event, since that route has no boundary above it.
userStories.notes: [P2][Frontend/Observability] Found 2026-07-18 by the frontend deep dive. ~5 lines. Worth pairing with US-2001 (the edge ships release='dev'), because both are the same failure: an error reaches production and nothing can attribute it. Credit where due — the audit rated the error-boundary layering as genuinely enterprise-grade (root/dashboard/buyer coverage plus a stale-chunk reload guard in main.tsx:21-26, a white-screen class most teams ship with); this is the one seam it misses. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). RouteErrorFallback now calls useRouteError() + captureException in a useEffect, matching what the class ErrorBoundary already did. One thing the audit did not mention and that matters: useRouteError() also surfaces THROWN RESPONSES (a 404/500 from a loader), which are not Error instances — captured raw, Sentry would have recorded '[object Object]'. Normalized so a thrown Response becomes 'Route error: HTTP <status> <statusText>' and anything else stringifies usefully. Tagged source=RouteErrorFallback with the pathname in extra, because the whole point is /embed/grade/:id — mounted OUTSIDE RootLayout with no class boundary above it — where knowing WHERE it fired is the difference between a triaged partner outage and a mystery. Verified: tsc -b clean, 2232 vitest tests, build green. STILL passes:false on AC2: I did not force a real embed-route error and confirm the Sentry event arrives. Worth doing, and note it is gated on VITE_SENTRY_DSN being set (sentry.ts:63 no-ops without it) — same class of 'configured?' question as US-2001/US-2003.

userStories.title: Dialog height overrides regress dvh to vh — the plan picker and credit-pack CTAs can sit under mobile browser chrome
userStories.description: As a mobile buyer, the purchase button must be reachable. Prioritize the two revenue dialogs (plan picker, credit pack).
Consider whether the override is needed at all, given the base is already correct.
userStories.notes: [P2][Frontend/Revenue] Found 2026-07-18 by the frontend deep dive. Effectively a find-and-replace, but it sits directly on the payment path, which is why it outranks several larger items. userStories.title: Nightly equity snapshot is 5 sequential round trips per seller and will silently stop scaling
userStories.description: As GradeThread, the equity trend must not quietly go flat. jobs-equity-snapshot.ts:60 loops over owners calling computeEquityForOwner (:62) plus a per-owner upsert (:63-76). computeEquityForOwner (flipdesk-equity.ts:118) issues per owner: sales then listings for personalSellThroughDays (:78-83 then :90-94, genuinely dependent), inventory_items (:122-127), and listings (:128-131, NO limit, whole tenant history). So 4 queries + 1 upsert = 5 sequential round trips per owner, with owner discovery capped at OWNER_SCAN_CAP = 20_000. Separately :44-48 scans inventory_items GLOBALLY with .not('status','in',...) and no user filter, pulling up to 20,000 rows to dedupe user_id client-side — a nightly seq scan on the largest table (a NOT IN over four enum values will not use idx_inventory_items_status).
acceptanceCriteria: Discover owners with a SELECT DISTINCT user_id RPC instead of a global scan + client-side dedupe.
Process owners in bounded-concurrency chunks rather than fully sequentially.
Add a .limit() to the unbounded listings read at flipdesk-equity.ts:131.

Also fix the sibling pattern in jobs-portfolio-alerts.ts: :117-120 issues one UPDATE per closet item inside a per-buyer loop (500 buyers x 100 items = 50,000 sequential UPDATEs). lib/portfolio-valuation-db.ts:147-149 already does this correctly with a single batched .upsert — copy that.
userStories.notes: [P2][Perf/Cron] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. The failure is DELAYED and SILENT, which is what makes it worth filing now: at 5,000 sellers this is ~25,000 sequential round trips, roughly 500s at ~20ms each — inside the 1800s job lock today. It scales linearly and blows the lock at ~10k sellers, at which point snapshots simply stop and the equity trend chart goes flat with no error. Compounds with US-2004 (nothing alerts on a stalled cron) — this job could stop and nobody would know. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC2 + AC3 + AC4 done. (AC3) flipdesk-equity.ts:131 now carries .limit(INVENTORY_CAP) — the inventory read beside it was always capped while this one pulled the owner's ENTIRE listing history including long-sold rows, on a path the nightly job runs for every seller; it only feeds a listed_at lookup for CURRENT inventory, so a listing with no matching unsold item contributes nothing and the same cap is the right bound. (AC2) jobs-equity-snapshot.ts now processes owners in chunks of 8 via Promise.allSettled instead of one at a time — ~5 round trips per owner serially was ~25,000 sequential round trips at 5,000 sellers (~500s at 20ms), inside the 1800s lock today but scaling linearly to blow it around 10k sellers, at which point snapshots SILENTLY stop and the equity trend goes flat. Concurrency 8 is deliberately modest: reads plus one idempotent upsert (onConflict user_id,snapshot_date), so ordering is irrelevant and retries are harmless, but this shares Postgres with live traffic and a nightly job has no business saturating it. (AC4) jobs-portfolio-alerts.ts inner loop chunked the same way. ⚠ I DID NOT use the batched upsert the AC suggested, and the reason matters: peak_estimate_cents differs per row AND the update SHAPE differs (only alerting rows carry last_alert_estimate_cents/last_alerted_at), so a single upsert would need every column for every row and would INSERT a partial row for anything missing from closet_item_valuations rather than updating it. Setting distinct per-row values in one statement needs a VALUES join — an RPC and a migration. Concurrency gets most of the win with none of that risk. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4178 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false on AC1: owner discovery still scans inventory_items globally with .not(status,in,...) and dedupes user_id client-side (a nightly seq scan on the largest table, since NOT IN over four enum values will not use idx_inventory_items_status). The fix is a SELECT DISTINCT user_id RPC, which needs a migration, and I did not want to stack a third held one.

userStories.title: GDPR data export materializes a seller's entire commercial history in one isolate
userStories.description: As the largest sellers, our data export must not be the one thing that cannot run. services/edge-functions/src/routes/account.ts:221-227 selects grade_reports (.in submissionIds), listings (.eq user_id) and sales (.eq user_id) with select('*') and no bound, assembling everything into one in-memory payload (:230+). Correctly parallelized and correctly tenant-scoped, and it is a rare user-initiated action — but it is the most likely OOM in the service, and it fails for exactly the largest (most valuable) accounts. Same file :378-381 fetches submissions.select('id') and inventory_items.select('id') purely to COUNT them; duplicated at admin-compliance.ts:474 and lib/support-tools.ts:77,96,396.
acceptanceCriteria: Stream the export to storage as NDJSON and return a signed URL, rather than building the whole payload in memory.
Replace the count-by-fetching-ids patterns with count:'exact', head:true.
Test against a seeded heavy account — the failure mode only appears at the size where it matters.
userStories.notes: [P3][Perf/Compliance] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. P3 because it is rare and user-initiated, but note the compliance angle: an export that OOMs for large accounts is a GDPR access-request failure for precisely the users most likely to file one. Related and already fixed this session: US-2005 added the email-keyed purge to the DELETE path in this same file. | 2026-07-18 ⚠ TWO OF THE FOUR CITED SITES ARE WRONG — correcting the story rather than 'fixing' working code (agent loop). The audit claimed account.ts:378-381 and admin-compliance.ts:474 'fetch every row purely to count them' and should be count:'exact',head:true. FALSE, verified by reading both: the ids are NOT counted, they are USED — fed straight into .in('submission_id', subIds) / .in('inventory_item_id', itemIds) to derive STORAGE PATHS before the cascade deletes the rows. Replacing them with head-counts would BREAK deletion by leaving orphaned storage objects, which is exactly the GDPR failure US-2005 was about. A head:true count returns no rows at all. support-tools.ts:77 (ownedItemIds) is likewise legitimate — it returns ids used for scoping. The ONE genuine instance is support-tools.ts:96 getMyInventoryStatusCounts, which selects status for every item to group client-side; a proper fix is a GROUP BY, which PostgREST cannot express without an RPC (parallel per-status head-counts over the fixed ITEM_STATUSES set is the migration-free alternative). Left unfixed: it is a support-tooling path, not a hot one, and I would rather record an accurate finding than churn code to close a mostly-wrong AC. The MAIN finding — the export at :221-227 materializing a seller's whole commercial history in one isolate — STANDS and is untouched; streaming to storage as NDJSON is a real change and belongs in its own pass. LESSON worth keeping: this is the second audit claim this session that did not survive verification (the first was US-2024's 'unbounded batch', which had a .max(200) all along). Read the code before acting on a finding, even a well-argued one.

userStories.title: Affiliate commissions and hardcoded USD — two unreversed/unchecked money assumptions
userStories.description: Two SUSPECTED money issues from the same audit, filed together because both need a business answer before code. (1) AFFILIATE CLAWBACK: lib/affiliate-payout.ts has a hold_until window (default 30 days, affiliate-payout-math.ts:61) but no refund/chargeback reversal — a referred subscription refunded on day 31+ leaves the commission paid. Whether the hold is sufficient depends on the real refund-age distribution, which was not checkable from source. (2) CURRENCY: consignor-payout.ts:325 hardcodes currency 'usd' with Math.round(amount * 100). The main sales table (00008) has NO currency column, so it is self-consistent TODAY — but 00101_flipdesk_ebay_orphan_sales.sql:21 and 00327_ebay_payouts.sql:14 DO carry currency, and flipdesk-ebay.ts:1955 defaults line items to 'USD'. A non-US eBay site would write GBP/EUR amounts into a currency-less decimal and transfer them as USD.
acceptanceCriteria: Affiliate: measure the actual refund-age distribution, then either extend the hold, add a clawback, or record the accepted loss with the number attached.

Currency: decide whether non-US marketplaces are in scope. If yes, sales needs a currency column and every money path needs to stop assuming USD. If no, add a guard that REJECTS a non-USD sale rather than silently treating it as dollars.
Do not fix the currency assumption piecemeal — a half-migrated currency model is worse than an explicit single-currency one.
userStories.notes: [P2][Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the money deep dive, both filed as SUSPECTED rather than confirmed. The currency one is the classic slow-burn: it is correct today and silently wrong the moment someone connects a UK or EU eBay account, with no error — just wrong amounts. Also captured from the same audit, not filed separately: ai-metering.ts:101-108 refunds a reserved AI action only in its catch block, so an isolate kill strands the reservation — but impact is bounded and self-healing, since webhooks.ts:868-877 zeroes ai_actions_used_this_month each cycle. Worth knowing, not worth a story.

userStories.title: Grading wizard destroys staged photos on navigation with no warning
userStories.description: As a seller mid-submission, leaving the wizard must not silently discard the photos I just shot. src/pages/new-submission.tsx autosaves form fields and a photo MANIFEST (name + type) but never the binaries — a deliberate and correct choice, since multi-MB Files cannot live in localStorage. The consequence is that staged photos exist only in React state, and NOTHING guarded the exit: there was no useBlocker anywhere in the repo (zero hits) and beforeunload existed only in stores/autolister-upload-store.ts:867, not on this wizard. A seller who staged 8 photos and clicked any sidebar link, or refreshed, lost all of them with no prompt — and handleResumeDraft deliberately caps resume at step 1, forcing full photo re-entry.
acceptanceCriteria: Guard BOTH escape routes: in-app navigation (useBlocker, which can show a real dialog) and page unload (beforeunload, where the browser shows its own generic prompt). Neither alone is sufficient.
Block only while there is genuinely something to lose — a guard that fires when nothing is at stake trains people to click through it.
Say what will be lost, with the count. 'Unsaved changes' is easy to dismiss; '8 photos' is not.
userStories.notes: [P1][Frontend/Data-loss] Found 2026-07-18 by the frontend deep dive, which called it 'the single most expensive failure in the app: photo capture is the highest-effort step of the highest-value journey'. FIXED SAME PASS: added src/hooks/use-navigation-guard.ts (useBlocker + beforeunload, with a reset when the condition clears so a user is never stranded behind a dialog about work that no longer exists) and wired it into new-submission.tsx gated on photos.length > 0 && !isSubmitting — the isSubmitting half matters, or the guard traps the caller behind their own success navigation. The dialog names the exact photo count. Verified: tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, 481 lib tests pass, npm run build prerenders 213 routes. STILL passes:false: not driven in a real browser. The behaviours worth confirming by hand are (a) sidebar click while photos are staged shows the dialog, (b) 'Keep editing' leaves state intact, (c) submitting navigates WITHOUT the prompt, (d) refresh shows the browser's own warning.

userStories.title: Credit-pack refund clawback was keyed per CHARGE while the amount was CUMULATIVE
userStories.description: As GradeThread, a partially-refunded credit pack must not leave the customer holding both the credits and the money. webhooks.ts computed the clawback from charge.amount_refunded (CUMULATIVE for the charge) but keyed the ledger reversal on the CHARGE id. Stripe fires charge.refunded once per refund and revoke_grade_credits no-ops on a repeated key, so on a second refund the amount was right and the write was SKIPPED. On a $50 / 50-credit pack: refund $10 (10 credits revoked, key claimed), later refund the remaining $40 (clawback computes 50, key already used, NO-OP) — the customer keeps all $50 AND 40 credits. admin-billing.ts's admin-refund:<charge>:<amount> path deliberately permits exactly that second partial refund, so this was reachable by design, not by accident.
acceptanceCriteria: Key the ledger reversal on the REFUND, not the charge, and pass that refund's INCREMENTAL amount.
Keep US-892's property intact: admin-billing's direct ledger call must use the same per-refund key, so whichever path runs first still wins and the other no-ops.
Add the missing Stripe idempotency key on the downgrade-proration refund.

userStories.notes: [P1][Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the money-correctness deep dive. FIXED SAME PASS, all four ACs. Both sides had to move together. Fallback kept for the case where Stripe omits the refunds list: revert to cumulative/per-charge, which under-claws (the pre-existing bug) rather than never clawing — strictly better than skipping. ALSO FIXED: the downgrade-proration refund (admin-billing.ts:215) was the ONLY Stripe money-mover with no idempotency key, protected purely by ACCIDENT (the subscription cancel above throws first on a retry) — not a guarantee, just an ordering nobody is obliged to preserve. And grade-billing.ts's credits + super-admin flips now carry .eq('user_id', userId) like their US-1638-hardened sibling. 4 new tests pin the increments-sum-to-the-grant property and the clamps. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4173 edge tests pass. STILL passes:false: source-only. userStories.title: Golden set leaked into few-shot exemplars — every exemplar eval number was suspect
userStories.description: Train/test contamination in the grading engine. Golden eval cases are grown from corrected human reviews (grading-eval.ts promoteGradeReportToEvalCase records the origin in grading_eval_cases.source_grade_report_id), and few-shot exemplars are mined from THE SAME corrected reviews (few-shot-exemplars.ts assembleExemplarSet) with no cross-exclusion. So one corrected report could be both a golden case and an exemplar in the prompt block. evalExemplarSet then gates a candidate exemplar set against the golden set it may contain — the model was shown the answers to the cases it was scored on.
acceptanceCriteria: Exclude golden-set sources from the exemplar pool (DONE 2026-07-18).
Backfill question: any exemplar set activated BEFORE this fix was gated against a possibly-contaminated eval. Re-run the gate for currently-active sets and confirm they still clear honestly.
If any published accuracy figure cites evalThresholds(), restate it after the re-run.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Correctness] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive; I VERIFIED it myself before acting (source_grade_report_id does exist on grading_eval_cases, and a grep for any exclusion in few-shot-exemplars.ts returned nothing). FIXED SAME PASS: assembleExemplarSet now loads all non-null source_grade_report_ids and filters them out of the exemplar pool, logging how many were excluded so the effect is visible. It fails CLOSED if that lookup errors — assembling a set while unable to prove it is uncontaminated produces a number nobody can trust, which defeats the gate's entire purpose. Excludes ALL golden sources rather than only active cases: an inactive case can be reactivated, and a set contaminated at assembly time cannot be decontaminated afterwards. STILL passes:false, and this is the important part — the CODE is fixed but the DATA question is not. Exemplar sets activated before today were gated against a possibly-contaminated eval, so their measured quality may be fictitious; that needs a re-run against the now-clean pool, which needs prod data. Exemplar PRIVACY was separately verified clean: the selects carry only garment_type/garment_category/scores/intentional_misread — no review notes, titles, user ids or photos.

userStories.title: Grading determinism (US-481) is void on the default model, and the code still claims it
userStories.description: ai-config.ts:157-179 documents that grading ALWAYS uses a low temperature, defaulting to 0 (fully greedy decoding), because a certified score backs a public 'standardized' value prop. But gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort — not temperature — for effort-based models, and the default grading model (DEFAULTS.model = claude-sonnet-5) is effort-based. So getGradingTemperature() is never called on the shipping path, GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE and the whole clamping apparatus are dead code, and grading runs at the model's own non-greedy decoding. A regrade of the same photos can return a different score with no explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE the product position: is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? That is a trust question, not an engineering one.
If determinism is still the promise: add a self-consistency check (grade twice, compare, flag divergence) or pin a decoding mode that guarantees it.

If it is NOT the promise: correct the ai-config.ts comment block, which currently asserts a property the code does not have, and disclose run-to-run variance wherever the 'standardized grade' claim is made.
Either way the comment must stop describing temperature clamping as though it governs grading.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. I VERIFIED the mechanism myself: DEFAULTS.model is claude-sonnet-5 (ai-config.ts:12), modelUsesEffort() matches it (:189-192), and gradingSamplingParams() returns the effort branch with no temperature (:228-233). This is NOT a code bug — effort-based models do not accept temperature, so the US-1033 migration was a correct API fix. The defect is that it silently removed a DOCUMENTED GUARANTEE and nobody updated the guarantee. Code that claims a property it no longer has is the most dangerous state for a trust product, because everyone downstream reasons from the claim rather than the behaviour. I deliberately did not 'fix' it: the right answer is a product decision — restore determinism (costly, possibly not available on this model family) or stop promising it (cheap, but it changes what a certificate means).

userStories.title: The eval gate pins the PROMPT but not the MODEL — an env change bypasses it entirely
userStories.description: activatePromptVersion (grading-eval.ts:568-580) gates on a boolean eval_passed stamped at :342 with no model attribution, while the grading model is pure env config: getDefaultModel() returns DEFAULT_AI_MODEL with no gate. The allowlist comment (ai-config.ts:65) says to extend it 'when a new model is qualified against the eval gate' — convention, not code. So an operator can point DEFAULT_AI_MODEL at another allowlisted model via a Coolify env change (no deploy, no eval, no audit entry, no step-up) and every subsequent paid grade comes from a model that never cleared MAE/agreement thresholds, while the prompt version still reads eval_passed:true from a run against a different model.
acceptanceCriteria: Record the qualifying model on the version's pass stamp (grading_eval_runs already stores it at grading-eval.ts:322) and have activatePromptVersion compare it against the live grading model.
Refuse to grade — or at minimum emit a critical ops event — when the live model differs from the model the active prompt version was qualified on.
Treat a model change as an auditable event: today it leaves no trace at all.
userStories.notes: [P2][Grading/Governance] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive (structurally confirmed; the operational scenario is inferred). Worth recording what IS well built, because the contrast is the finding: prompt activation and canary both require step-up, both audit-log, both invalidate the prompt cache, and NO route mutates prompt_text after creation — so the 'pass eval, then edit the text, then activate' attack does not exist. The prompt half of this lifecycle is genuinely solid. The model half has no gate whatsoever.

userStories.title: Golden eval cases are hard-deletable and freely editable with no step-up
userStories.description: The grading-engine skill states: 'Never delete cases to make an eval pass. A shrinking golden set is a red flag in review.' Nothing enforces it. admin-grading.ts PATCH /eval/cases/:id updates expected_score/expected_tier/tags/is_active with no restriction on who or why, and DELETE /eval/cases/:id is a HARD delete rather than a soft is_active=false. Neither route calls requireStepUp — unlike /prompts/:id/activate, /prompts/:id/canary and /review/:id/adjust, which all do.
acceptanceCriteria: Soft-delete instead of hard-delete, so a removed case stays auditable.
Require step-up on both mutate and delete, matching the other grading-governance routes.
Alert (or log at critical) when the ACTIVE golden set shrinks — that is the signal the skill actually asks reviewers to watch for, and a human watching a table is not a mechanism.
Consider making expected_score immutable once a case has appeared in a passing run: editing it retroactively invalidates historical comparisons.
userStories.notes: [P2][Grading/Governance] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. Mitigations that DO exist: both routes write auditLog, and grading_eval_runs snapshots per_case results, so a historical run's contents remain forensically recoverable. The exposure is that an operator can nudge a stubborn prompt version past the gate by deleting or re-scoring the cases it fails and then activating it against live customer traffic — and cross-run accuracy comparisons silently stop being comparable, because the denominator moved underneath them.

Same class as US-1998 (a gate that fails early hides every gate behind it) seen from the other side: a gate that SKIPS silently is indistinguishable from one that passes. userStories.notes: [P1][Security/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the test-suite deep dive. This is the least-covered critical path in the product: auth / session / workspace-member. A regression letting a VIEWER spend the owner's credits would ship green — and 'C3: viewer cannot pay for a grade' is exactly the test that would have caught it, sitting there skipped. Pairs directly with US-2014, which added new cases to this same suite: those cases are only as good as the fixture that enables them, so this story is what makes that one real. | 2026-07-18 AC1 + AC2 FIXED (agent loop). The seed script now creates tenant-viewer@tenant-isolation.test and UPSERTS a role=viewer workspace_members row for tenant A, then emits TEST_VIEWER_JWT + TEST_WORKSPACE_OWNER_ID; both are now in REQUIRED_RESOURCE_IDS, so a missing viewer fixture FAILS CI instead of skipping seven cases silently. ⚠ THE STORY'S COLUMN NAMES WERE WRONG and I checked rather than pasted: it said workspace_owner_id / member_user_id; the actual schema (00042) is owner_id / member_id, with UNIQUE(owner_id, member_id), CHECK(owner_id <> member_id) and CHECK(role <> 'owner'). Upserting on that unique constraint keeps the seed idempotent AND resets a role a previous run may have changed, rather than duplicating the row. Worth being explicit about WHY the viewer is a third user rather than reusing B: they prove different things. B is a FOREIGN tenant (cross-tenant isolation — 'you cannot touch another account's data'); V is legitimately INSIDE A's workspace (intra-workspace role enforcement — 'you may act here but may not spend the owner's money'). Conflating them would have left the second property untested, which is exactly the hole. NO WORKFLOW CHANGE NEEDED: tenant-isolation.yml already pipes the seed's KEY=value output into GITHUB_ENV, so the two new vars flow through automatically. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by simulating CI — TENANT_ISOLATION_REQUIRED=1 with all twelve original ids present but the viewer absent now fails with 'seeded resource ids missing, cross-tenant cases would SKIP: TEST_VIEWER_JWT, TEST_WORKSPACE_OWNER_ID'. Verified: deno check + lint clean (1183 files), 4185 edge tests pass. userStories.title: Stand up vault/ skeleton and the note frontmatter contract
userStories.description: As an agent working in this repo, I want a single navigable knowledge root with a machine-checkable note schema, so that retrieval is one predictable surface instead of 203 scattered markdown files with no index.
acceptanceCriteria: vault/ created at repo root with numbered top-level folders: 00-index, 10-ops, 20-domain (with brands/), 30-platform, 40-growth, 50-business, 60-decisions, 70-agent, 90-archive.
vault/.obsidian/ committed with wikilink resolution set to shortest-path-when-possible and the graph configured so folder = colour group.
vault/CONTRACT.md documents the frontmatter schema and is the ONLY place the schema is defined (no restating in CLAUDE.md).

Frontmatter schema: title, type (runbook|contract|reference|decision|learning|moc), status (current|superseded|archived), source_of_truth (code|vault), code_refs (list of repo-relative paths), reviewed (ISO date), tags.

source_of_truth:code means the note DESCRIBES code and the code wins on conflict; source_of_truth:vault means the note is authoritative (decisions, runbooks, taxonomy). This distinction drives the US-2044 drift guard — do not collapse it.
At least one hand-authored seed note per top-level folder so the schema is exercised, not just specified.
No existing docs are moved in this story — skeleton only.
userStories.notes: [EPIC: Knowledge Vault] Karpathy-style agentic wiki — markdown navigation, NO vector DB / embeddings. The value is CONSOLIDATION (203 md files today, with real duplicates); the Obsidian layer is packaging. Every migration story is a MOVE with a redirect stub, never a copy — mirroring would double drift and save zero tokens. Phase 1 (foundation). Folder numbering is deliberate: it sorts in both Obsidian's file explorer and `ls`, and gives wikilinks a stable prefix. code_refs is the load-bearing field — it is what makes staleness DETECTABLE rather than a matter of discipline.

userStories.title: vault-lint: frontmatter + wikilink parser and rule engine

Prints a ✓/✗ summary matching the house style of scripts/verify.mjs.

userStories.description: As a human reading the vault in Obsidian, I want it to use Obsidian idiom properly — live queries, transclusion, callouts, aliases — so that it is a real Obsidian vault rather than a folder of markdown that Obsidian happens to open.
acceptanceCriteria: AUDIT (2026-07-19, 60 notes): 281 wikilinks and full frontmatter, but ZERO embeds, ZERO block refs, ZERO aliases, ZERO callouts, ZERO Dataview/Bases, 1 heading-link out of 281, no plugins installed, and 47 hand-written Related sections duplicating what the backlinks pane gives free. Roughly 40% Obsidian-native.

PURE WINS (no downside for either reader): convert hand-rolled "> **WARNING ...**" blocks to real callouts (> [!warning] / [!info] / [!danger]) — they render natively AND grep as plain text; add aliases: to notes with common alternate names (frontmatter only, invisible to agents); use heading links [[note#section]] where a section is meant, currently 1 of 281.
LIVE VIEWS: add Dataview (or core Bases) views — all contract notes, notes by reviewed-date staleness, notes by tag, orphan risk. Install the plugin(s) into .obsidian and commit the config.

DUAL-CONSUMER RULE — the design constraint, do not skip. An agent reading raw markdown CANNOT run a Dataview query and does NOT see embedded content: ![[pricing#Credit packs]] greps as link text, not as 4.99. Live views are therefore ADDED ALONGSIDE the generated INDEX.md, never replacing it, and vault-index.mjs stays. Humans get the live view, agents get the materialized one, both from the same frontmatter.

TRANSCLUSION with eyes open: use ![[note#section]] where a fact genuinely must not be duplicated (the price table is the obvious case). For each embed, confirm the consuming note still carries enough surrounding context that an agent landing there via Grep is not stranded.

Convert the 47 hand-written Related sections to a generated or Dataview-backed backlinks view, OR keep them and add a lint rule that they are complete — nothing verifies one today, so they will rot silently.

Validate the graph by ACTUALLY OPENING Obsidian: per-folder colour groups work, no disconnected islands, no more than a handful of hubs above ~20 links. It was configured blind in US-2042 and never checked.
Record the dual-consumer decision as an ADR in vault/60-decisions, so nobody deletes vault-index.mjs as redundant once Bases exists.
vault-lint still passes, and verify:vault still catches a dangling link, an orphan, a stale index and contract drift after conversion.
