userStories.title: iOS: full-resolution JPEG encode runs on the main actor, once per shutter press
userStories.description: ios/GradeThread/Capture/CameraSession.swift:296-309 — the class is @MainActor (line 10-11) and deliver() is called from a @MainActor hop (line 291-293), so photo.fileDataRepresentation() (line 302) and UIImage(data:) (line 303) both run on the main thread. The shot is explicitly configured for maximum quality (AVVideoCodecType.jpeg at 206-208, quality prioritization clamped to the output ceiling at 214-219), so this is a full-sensor-resolution JPEG serialization on the main thread. The irony in context: PhotoIntakeView.capture() at line 958 deliberately calls PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain with the comment 'US-636: compress off the main actor' — but the UIImage it receives was ALREADY produced by a main-thread encode. The expensive half was paid before the optimized half began.
acceptanceCriteria: Move the encode off the main actor: do fileDataRepresentation() + UIImage(data:) inside a Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated) in photoOutput(_:didFinishProcessingPhoto:) — it is already nonisolated, so this is a small change — and hop to @MainActor only to call finishPendingCapture with the finished UIImage.
The watchdog at 199-204 keys on pendingCaptureID and is unaffected; confirm that still holds after the change.

MEASURE the encode duration on-device before and after. The main-thread claim is confirmed from the isolation annotations; the magnitude is inferred from the operation and the quality settings, and should not be assumed.
userStories.notes:
[P1][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the first iOS audit this repo has had. Symptom: a visible hitch on EVERY shutter tap — shutter animation and slot-strip update stutter. Grading requires 4+ photos per item, so a seller feels it 4+ times per item and continuously in bulk capture; it is the app's most-repeated interaction. NOT FIXED HERE, deliberately: Swift cannot be built or tested on this Windows checkout (repo guidance is explicit that xcodebuild is macOS-only and only ios/Scripts/no-ungated-print.py runs locally), and an unverifiable edit to the camera path — the highest-volume, hardest-to-debug surface in the app — is not worth the risk. Needs a macOS session. Worth knowing the surrounding code is otherwise strong: US-635 downsampling, US-636 off-main compression, US-1165/1166 off-main parse + size caps are all in place, which is exactly why this one site stands out.

STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-18 — THIS FINDING WAS WRONG. Verified against the source: PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain (US-636) already exists precisely so "@MainActor callers (capture, library import, snap) never block the UI on a full-resolution encode", and EVERY production call site uses compressOffMain or compressBatch — PhotoIntakeView (the shutter path) at :909 and :958, AutoListerReviewModel :220/:812, ItemCanvasView :1731/:1759, PhotoRotateService :90, PhotosDropHandler :20, ProspectStore :97, ReconcileIntakeView :143. The ONLY caller of the synchronous compress() is GradeThreadTests/PhotoIntakeTests.swift:12. There is no per-shutter main-actor encode; the premise of this story does not exist. Closing as invalid rather than leaving a P1 that would have sent someone to a Mac to fix nothing.

The audit was not entirely empty, though: the scan for main-actor encodes did surface ONE real raw-encode site (PostSaleView dispute evidence), which is fixed under US-2083 — a different and much smaller defect than the one claimed here.

userStories.title: iOS: AutoLister ungrouped pool is a non-lazy stack that re-sorts up to 200 photos per render
userStories.description: Two compounding problems in ios/GradeThread/AutoLister/AutoListerView.swift:352-358. (a) Line 353 is HStack, not LazyHStack, so every ungrouped photo's view is materialized however far off-screen; the batch cap is maxBatchPhotos = 200 (AutoListerReviewModel.swift:168) and the ungrouped pool can hold all 200, since ungrouping to re-sort is its documented purpose (:377-384). (b) ungroupedSorted (AutoListerReviewModel.swift:403-445) is a COMPUTED property doing an O(n log n) sort — building a Set, filtering importOrder, compactMapping into structs, then stableSorted with a per-comparison provenance/numeric comparator — and it is read directly inside body, so it re-runs on EVERY body evaluation, including ones triggered by unrelated @Published churn (isImporting, verifying, verifyProgress, proposing, proposeProgress, capNotice, actionError, suggestions, proposalReviews, aiActionsRemaining — lines 52-95).
acceptanceCriteria: Change line 353 to LazyHStack. (The sibling groupCard at 556-562 has the same non-lazy HStack but groups are individually small — that one is benign; the ungrouped pool is the one that scales.)

Memoize ungroupedSorted: either the InventoryDerivation pattern (a non-observable final class cache keyed on ungrouped + ungroupedSort + importOrder) or recompute in the didSet of ungrouped/ungroupedSort and store it as a plain stored property.
Verify with Instruments on a 200-photo batch, specifically during an AI verify/propose pass — those publish progress per window (lines 78, 80), which is when the re-sort storm is worst.
userStories.notes:
[P1][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the iOS audit. Symptom: dropped frames scrolling the ungrouped strip on a large batch, plus stutter during AI verify/propose — each progress publish re-sorts up to 200 photos AND rebuilds up to 200 views. The instructive part is that this problem was already SOLVED elsewhere in the same app: InventoryListView uses InventoryDerivation memoization and its header comment (Inventory/InventoryDerivation.swift:6-13) describes this precise failure mode. AutoLister never got the same treatment. NOT FIXED HERE — Swift is unbuildable/untestable on Windows; needs a macOS session.

VERIFIED + PARTIALLY FIXED 2026-07-18. Both halves of the claim hold, but their WEIGHTS were wrong and the fix is smaller than the story implied.

Confirmed: AutoListerView:353 wrapped the ungrouped pool in a plain HStack, so every one of up to ~200 thumbnails was realized including off-screen ones, and each AI verify/propose progress publish re-rendered the strip. ungroupedSorted (AutoListerReviewModel:403) is indeed a computed property doing Set + filter + compactMap + sort on every body evaluation.

Correction to my own framing: the re-SORT is not the problem. 200 items is ~1,500 comparisons — microseconds. The dominant cost was building 200 SwiftUI views. So the fix is LazyHStack, and the InventoryDerivation-style memoization this story asked for is very likely unnecessary micro-optimisation. Not doing it.

Fixed: HStack -> LazyHStack at the ungrouped pool only. LazyVStack/LazyHStack are already established here (AutoListerView:219 in the same file; InventoryBoardView:34-35 documents the identical reasoning for a 500+-item catalog). The per-group strip at :557 deliberately stays a plain HStack — a group is one item photos, typically 4-12, where laziness costs more than it saves.

⚠️ NOT COMPILE-VERIFIED (Windows checkout). One-word change to a SwiftUI container used elsewhere in the same file; iOS CI on macOS is the real check.

userStories.title: iOS: bulk photo import is strictly serial though a bounded-concurrency helper already exists
userStories.description: Both PHPicker import paths — AutoListerReviewModel.swift:218-243 and PhotoIntakeView.swift:907-923 — are plain serial for loops awaiting per photo: result.loadImage() (I/O; for iCloud-backed photos a NETWORK round trip each), then PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain (CPU), then a detached DHash.compute (CPU, :238-240). Meanwhile PhotoCompressor.compressBatch(_:maxConcurrent:) (PhotoCompressor.swift:64-91) exists for exactly this — bounded concurrency, per-item autoreleasepool, order-preserving — and a grep of the whole ios/ tree shows its ONLY caller is Inventory/PhotosDropHandler.swift:20. Neither high-volume import path uses it.
acceptanceCriteria: Wrap the whole per-photo unit (load + compress + dHash) in the chunked withTaskGroup shape already used correctly three times in this codebase: PhotoCompressor.compressBatch, DisclosureStore.renderAll (Disclosure/DisclosureStore.swift:88-115) and ReconciliationService (:215-242).

Keep concurrency modest (3-4) so only a few full-resolution UIImages are resident — that memory property is why compressBatch was written, and parallelising without it trades a latency win for a jetsam risk.
Preserve input order via the enumerate-and-sort approach at DisclosureStore.swift:106.
userStories.notes:
[P2][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the iOS audit. The dominant cost is loadImage(), not compression: for iCloud-backed photos that is a serialized network fetch per photo, so a 200-photo import is 200 sequential round trips. Symptom: bulk import sits on the spinner for minutes rather than tens of seconds when photos are not local, and it widens the window for the 'still downloading from iCloud' partial-failure path the code already anticipates (:255-259). NOT FIXED HERE — Swift is unbuildable on Windows.

VERIFIED 2026-07-18 — REAL, still open, deliberately NOT fixed blind.

Confirmed at PhotoIntakeView.ingestLibraryPicks (:907): a plain `for result in results` loop awaiting result.loadImage() then compressOffMain per item. Strictly serial, so 200 iCloud-backed photos are 200 sequential network round trips.

Refinement to the story premise: the existing helper CANNOT be applied directly. PhotoCompressor.compressBatch takes [UIImage] — images already in memory — while the bottleneck is loadImage() upstream of it. What compressBatch does provide is the exact PATTERN to copy: a windowed `withTaskGroup(of: (Int, T).self)` writing into a pre-sized results array, which preserves picker order (the loop comment notes order matters for the tray) and bounds residency.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT worth recording, because the obvious implementation is wrong: do NOT load all images first and then call compressBatch. compressBatch own header explains why — it keeps only a few full-resolution UIImages resident so a large drop does not spike memory into a jetsam kill. Loading 200 full-res UIImages up front reintroduces exactly that risk. The correct shape is ONE windowed TaskGroup where each task does loadImage + compress together, so at most maxConcurrent full-res images exist at any moment.

Why not fixed here: this is ~25 lines of NEW concurrent Swift on the bulk-import path, with ordering and memory-residency invariants, and it cannot be compiled or tested on this Windows checkout. That is a different risk class from the one-word LazyHStack change — needs a macOS session.

userStories.title: 16 independent dollars() helpers with divergent rounding; one showed a $24.99 pack as $25
userStories.description: src/ contains SIXTEEN separate `function dollars(cents)` definitions and they disagree: most use toFixed(2), two use toFixed(0), one omits the leading $, one takes a currency, one returns 'Free' for 0, one handles null. The divergence is only SOMETIMES a bug, which is what makes it hard to see. FLIPDESK_PLANS are whole dollars (2900/5900/9900 monthly, 29000/59000/99000 yearly) so toFixed(0) on a plan card loses nothing and reads better. But CREDIT_PACKS (2499/5999/10999/19999) and GRADETHREAD_TIERS (299/799/1299/…) ALL carry cents, so rounding those invents money. The live instance: the landing page rendered a $24.99 pack as '$25' while /pricing rendered '$24.99' — the same pack at two prices on one site, on the page headlined 'transparent pricing'.
acceptanceCriteria: Consolidate to ONE money module with explicitly-named formatters — an exact one (money that carries cents: packs, tiers, payouts, P&L) and a deliberate whole-dollar one (plan cards) — so the choice is visible at the call site rather than implied by which local helper a file happened to define.
Audit the other 15 call sites for the same class of bug: any toFixed(0) applied to a value that can carry cents is money the display invents.
Keep the whole-dollar variant. $29/mo is better copy than $29.00/mo and loses nothing — the rule is about values that HAVE cents, not about decimals everywhere.
Extend the US-2075 guard from the landing call site to the shared formatter once it exists.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Money/Frontend] Found 2026-07-18 while pinning the pricing mirror (US-2019 AC2). The landing instance is FIXED and guarded (US-2075); this story is the systemic half. VERIFIED LIVE before and after: /pricing renders $24.99 / $59.99 / $109.99 / $199.99 while the landing pack section is CLIENT-RENDERED (only the $59 plan price appears in server HTML) — which is precisely why the discrepancy survived: it never showed up in a prerendered diff, so no HTML-level check could have caught it. Worth noting the direction of the error too: rounding UP advertises $25 and charges $24.99, which is harmless legally but erodes the exact 'transparent pricing' claim the page makes. The reverse — a surface rounding a $24.99 charge DOWN to $24 — would not be harmless, and with 16 divergent helpers nothing currently prevents it.

RESOLVED 2026-07-18 — narrower than filed. Enumerated all 16 helpers: 3 are input PARSERS (dollarsToCentsOrNull / dollarsFromCents), not display formatters, so the real population is 13. Of those, 12 use toFixed(2) and 3 use toFixed(0). The 3 whole-dollar ones are fed ONLY FLIPDESK_PLANS (2900/5900/9900, 29000/59000/99000 — all whole dollars), verified by reading every call site; landing's credit packs and grading tiers render via inline toFixed(2), not via its dollars(). So exactly ONE site was ever wrong (the $25-for-$24.99 pack) and it is already fixed.

Consolidating the remaining 12 identical toFixed(2) helpers is cosmetic duplication with no live defect, and a 16-file refactor is not worth the regression surface. Did the durable thing instead: src/lib/__tests__/money-display.test.ts now pins the invariant the safety actually rests on — (a) CREDIT_PACKS/GRADETHREAD_TIERS carry cents, (b) FLIPDESK_PLANS are whole dollars (so a future $29.99 plan fails loudly instead of silently rendering $30), (c) landing's pack block never uses toFixed(0), and (d) the two whole-dollar billing components never import a cents-bearing constant. Guard verified by sabotage: adding a CREDIT_PACKS import to flipdesk-plan-comparison.tsx turns it red; restored, 4/4 green.

userStories.title: SEO route registry shipped 89 KB gzipped of marketing prose in every page's eager bundle
userStories.notes:
Found while measuring web performance. public-routes.ts exports SITE_URL (194 refs) alongside PUBLIC_ROUTES (66 refs), which imports 17 route-data modules holding the marketing copy for all 213 public routes. Rollup hoisted those into one SHARED chunk, so any module importing the scalar inherited 305 KB raw / 89 KB gzip of prose — and seo.tsx + json-ld.ts are on every page, so it sat in the EAGER graph of every load, including landing, which renders none of it. The same copy was already in each route prerendered HTML, so it was pure duplication.

Fix: extracted the scalars to src/lib/seo/site.ts (zero imports), re-exported from public-routes.ts so the 66 registry consumers needed no change, and repointed the 16 scalar-only importers. Eager graph 305 -> 241 KB gzip (-64 KB on every page load, ~21%).

Verified no SEO regression: 213 routes still prerender, canonicals correct, all 7 custom OG images still emit (the rest legitimately use the default). Guard added at src/lib/seo/__tests__/site-leaf.test.ts, sabotage-verified on both edges (import added to site.ts; seo.tsx repointed back).

NOTE: the code landed as collateral in commit 85f68052 (a vault-migration commit from a concurrent agent session that ran git add -A). Only the guard test carries this reasoning.

VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-07-19: the landing page's eager script graph contains site-*.js (the new leaf) and NO public-routes chunk, so the 89 KB gzipped prose payload is off the critical path for every page.

userStories.title: 26 cross-tenant isolation cases cannot run in CI — the guard against silent skips only covered 14 of 38 gating ids

userStories.title: Three hub pages 404 in production — /blog, /authors and /condition-index were never routed to their Pages Functions
userStories.notes:
Found by auditing the SHIPPED prerendered HTML rather than the source. On-page SEO is clean (213 pages: no missing/duplicate titles or descriptions, no canonical mismatches, all inside truncation bands, no orphans), so the defect was in routing, not markup.

public/_routes.json listed only the WILDCARD for three surfaces — /blog/*, /authors/*, /condition-index/* — while each Pages Function also implements the BARE hub path (functions/blog/[[path]].ts line 77, authors line 53, condition-index line 164). Cloudflare never invoked the function for the bare URL, it fell through to static assets, and dist/_redirects ends in /* -> /404.html 404 with NO SPA fallback (the file comment states this explicitly). So all three returned hard 404s. The sibling surfaces /value and /durability each correctly listed both forms, which is what made the omission invisible by eye.

Impact: /condition-index is the cornerstone SEO destination (US-621, shipped and marked done) and is linked from the footer of ALL 213 public pages plus the HTML sitemap — 199 inbound internal links to a 404. /blog is the blog index and /authors the author index, both referenced by their own sitemaps and RSS.

Nothing could have caught this: the functions compile, their tests pass, the build succeeds, and every page renders correctly in local dev where _routes.json is not applied. It failed only in production, silently.

Fix: added the three bare paths. Guard at src/prerender/__tests__/pages-function-routing.test.ts derives the requirement — any functions/<name>/[[path]].ts that branches on the bare path must have it in _routes.json — plus a reverse check for route rules whose function no longer exists. The guard found /blog and /authors on its first run; I had only found /condition-index by hand. Sabotage-verified.

VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-07-19 after deploy: /blog, /authors and /condition-index all return 200. Sitemap spot-check confirms the harm was worse than filed — /condition-index and /blog are themselves listed as <loc> entries in sitemap-condition.xml and sitemap-blog.xml, so the site was actively SUBMITTING two hard-404 URLs to search engines, not merely linking to them internally. Sampled detail pages under both hubs (nike-vintage-tees, gap-denim-jacket, patagonia-synchilla, and three blog posts) all return 200, confirming only the bare hub paths were ever broken.

userStories.title: Physical-tag QR scans, passport claim links and the whole buyer portal 404 on cold load — no SPA fallback exists
userStories.notes:
Same root cause as US-2079, found by extending the reachability check from public pages to ROUTER routes. public/_redirects ends in /* -> /404.html 404 with NO SPA fallback rewrite (deliberate — it prevents soft-404 indexing). The consequence is that every client-rendered namespace needs either a spa-shell Pages Function or prerendered HTML. Four were missing:

1. /t/:code — physical-tag QR scan landing (US-1096). A QR scan is ALWAYS a cold direct load, so this surface was 100% non-functional in production. Every scan of every printed tag 404d.
2. /claim/:token — passport claim links, delivered by email or on a printed tag. Only ever opened as a direct load, so every claim link 404d.
3. /trust/:handle — opt-in public buyer Trust Score profile (US-1818), shared by link.
4. /buyer + 8 children (portfolio, billing, alerts, settings, rewards, onboarding, demand, guarantee) — the authenticated buyer portal. In-app navigation worked, so it looked healthy; refresh, bookmark or a shared link 404d.

Three of the four carried comments in src/routes/index.tsx describing a pure SPA route (no SSR Function) as a DELIBERATE choice. That is the misconception: it is only true on a host with a SPA fallback, and this one intentionally has none. The _redirects comment block explains this, and dashboard/admin/auth/login/signup/embed were each fixed for it previously (US-422) — these four were added later and missed.

Fix: four six-line spa-shell functions (functions/{buyer,claim,t,trust}/[[path]].ts) + the namespaces in _routes.json. serveSpaShell sends x-robots-tag: noindex, which is correct for all four (none are in PUBLIC_ROUTES).

Guard: pages-function-routing.test.ts now asserts every router route survives a cold load, resolving parameterised routes against prerendered instances (all 7 param SEO routes verified to have 9-138 prerendered slugs each, so an unknown slug correctly 404s). Sabotage-verified by removing /t/* and /buyer.

VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-07-19 after deploy: /t/testcode, /claim/testtoken, /trust/somehandle, /buyer and /buyer/portfolio all return 200 with x-robots-tag: noindex, nofollow — matching /dashboard, the reference implementation. The physical-tag QR surface is functional again.

userStories.title: SES/SNS signature verification could be disabled in prod on one of the two receivers — US-1641 hardened only half
userStories.notes:
Found by diffing env vars the code READS against env vars documented anywhere. Of 284 distinct vars, only 3 non-test vars were undocumented, and one was a security flag.

SES_SNS_SKIP_VERIFICATION exists so local dev can skip the outbound SNS cert fetch. US-1641 gated it on !isProduction() in routes/email-sns.ts specifically so a stray SES_SNS_SKIP_VERIFICATION=true in prod could not turn a public endpoint into a forgeable one. routes/webhooks.ts reads the SAME flag with NO production gate — while carrying a comment saying it Mirrors the canonical /api/email/ses-notifications receiver. The claim of a mirror was present; the mirror was not.

Both receivers are unauthenticated and act on arbitrary recipient addresses, so a forged bounce/complaint is a deliverability DoS: suppress mail to any address an attacker names. Not exploitable as shipped (the var is undocumented and almost certainly unset in prod, and isProduction was not even imported in webhooks.ts) — this is a latent hole and an incomplete security fix, not an active breach.

Fix: same !isProduction() gate. Guard at sns-skip-verify-gate_test.ts asserts EVERY read of the flag is conjoined with !isProduction(), and fails if fewer than 2 routes read it (so a rename cannot make it pass vacuously). Sabotage-verified by reverting webhooks.ts.

Also: documented all 3 undocumented runtime vars in vault/10-ops/env-reference.md (the flag plus VERIFIED_360_MIN_COVERAGE / VERIFIED_360_CONFIDENCE_BOOST, both of which have safe validated defaults of 0.85 and 0.1). vault:index + vault:lint clean.

userStories.title: Guard the US-1552 .or()-on-mutation rule, which CI structurally cannot catch
userStories.notes:
The self-hosted prod PostgREST rejects logical operators on UPDATE/DELETE with a 42703 naming the update-CTE alias; the NEWER PostgREST in the local Supabase stack accepts them. So verify:db boots the local stack, the query succeeds, CI goes green, and the failure only appears against prod. No amount of test EXECUTION can catch this — a source guard is the only available mechanism, which is why the rule had lived purely as prose in CLAUDE.md, the durable-jobs skill, and inline warnings in 7 source files, none of which can fail.

Scanned 2,137 files across src/, functions/ and services/edge-functions/src: currently ZERO violations, so this is pure regression prevention rather than a fix. Guard added at src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts covering update/delete/upsert, terminating each chain at the semicolon to avoid false positives from a later unrelated .or(), plus two vacuity checks (file count > 500, mutation-call count > 100) so a broken walk or regex fails loudly instead of passing empty. Sabotage-verified by adding the exact US-1552 pattern and watching it report file, line and snippet.

userStories.title: iOS: eBay dispute evidence uploaded without baking orientation — the one photo path that bypassed PhotoCompressor
userStories.notes:
[iOS] Found while VERIFYING US-2068 (which turned out to be a false positive). PostSaleView.handleEvidencePick encoded the picked photo with a bare image.jpegData(compressionQuality: 0.8), bypassing PhotoCompressor entirely.

Why it matters, in the codebase own words: PhotoCompressor.compress() calls normalizedUp() first because camera/library UIImages carry orientation as a FLAG with pixels in the sensor native rotation, and "consumers that ignore EXIF (eBay image pipeline does) then render them sideways/upside-down". This path uploads directly to eBay as DISPUTE EVIDENCE — a seller contesting a case, the highest-stakes photo in the product — so it could submit rotated evidence exactly when clarity matters most. It also skipped the 1600px/0.75 downscale (originals are 3-10 MB) and ran the encode on the MainActor, which the enclosing View Task inherits.

Checked the neighbours before generalising: the ONLY other raw encode is ShareExtension/ShareViewController.downscaledJPEG, which is correct and documented (US-1646) — the extension deliberately does not link the app target, and it bakes orientation upright via UIGraphicsImageRenderer and runs in Task.detached.

Fix: route through PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain, copying the call pattern used verbatim at 8 other sites. Gate added at ios/Scripts/no-raw-jpeg-encode.py (matching the existing no-force-unwrap / no-default-shared-session style), wired into ios-ci.yml, with a scanned-file-count floor so a layout change fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. Sabotage-verified: 410 files scanned, restoring the raw encode turns it red.

⚠️ NOT COMPILE-VERIFIED: Swift cannot be built on this Windows checkout. The edit is a 2-line substitution using an API called identically at 8 existing sites in the same module, so the risk is low, but iOS CI on macOS is the real check.

userStories.title: Two indexable marketing pages rendered with no nav or footer — /verified and /leaderboard shipped one outbound link each
userStories.notes:
Found by auditing conversion paths across the 213 prerendered pages: does every public page actually offer a route into the funnel?

/verified (the GradeThread Verified seller directory, US-863) and /leaderboard (public referrer leaderboard, US-864) rendered from a bare <div> + <SEO> instead of <MarketingLayout>, so neither had the site header or footer. Each shipped exactly ONE outbound link against 45 on a normal marketing page, and NO link to /signup.

Why it matters: /verified is a trust surface — it is where a buyer lands from a seller's shared Verified badge — and a visitor arriving there from search or a badge had no route to sign up and no way to navigate the site at all. Both pages also absorbed link equity from the sitewide footer (all 213 pages link to them) while passing essentially none back.

Also corrected a stale comment in referral-leaderboard.tsx asserting the page was 'NOT registered in PUBLIC_ROUTES (no prerender), like /status'. Both /leaderboard AND /status are in PUBLIC_ROUTES, indexable and prerendered. That note is exactly the kind that argues the next person out of giving an indexable page the chrome it needs.

Measured result after wrapping both in MarketingLayout: 1 outbound link -> 41, with a /signup path on each. Titles, descriptions and canonicals all still correct (MarketingLayout renders SEO itself, so the inner <SEO> was removed rather than duplicated).

DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED: /status, which the same audit flagged (2 links, both to /). A status page should render even when the app's shared chrome is broken, so keeping its dependencies minimal is the right call, not an oversight.

Verified end-to-end rather than by inspection: full rebuild + prerender, link counts measured from the emitted HTML, 2268 tests, tsc -b and eslint clean.

VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-07-19: /verified and /leaderboard each now serve 41 links including a /signup path, exactly matching the local measurement.

userStories.title: Edge auth/rate-limit coverage audited across all 865 route handlers — no gap found (negative result)
userStories.notes:
Systematic check of the Deno/Hono edge service: which of the 865 registered handlers are reachable without authentication, and of those, which are also unrated? Recorded so this is not repeated blindly.

RESULT: no defect. Coverage is sound. 101 handlers have no auth middleware, and every one is either intentionally public or protected in-handler:
  - health/metrics/ready — public by design
  - Stripe / SES / App Store / Google Play webhooks — signature-verified, not auth-gated
  - marketplace /oauth/callback (ebay, shopify, depop, etsy) — MUST be unauthenticated; the marketplace redirects a browser there, secured by the OAuth state parameter
  - /api/flipdesk/ebay/jobs/* and /api/notifications/trial-check — gated by requireJobSecret(), returning 401
  - /api/notifications/preferences — gated by verifyUnsubscribeToken(), correct for an emailed link
  - /api/v1/* — covered by apiKeyAuthMiddleware plus per-route scope checks
  - waitlist, guarantee claims, passport reads — public but rate-limited

STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION worth keeping, even though coverage is complete today: auth on the flipdesk and passport namespaces is applied as an ALLOWLIST of ~120 individual app.use() subpath patterns rather than a namespace wildcard, so a NEW handler added to one of those routers is unauthenticated by default until someone remembers to add a line to main.ts. That is fail-open. It has not bitten yet because in-handler guards (requireJobSecret, scope checks) cover the sensitive cases.

NO GUARD ADDED, deliberately. A reliable guard must model middleware patterns AND in-handler auth (requireJobSecret, token verification, scope checks) AND the legitimately-public set. My scan produced 832, then 114, then 101 candidate 'gaps' across four iterations — every one a tooling artifact (a bare /\.(get|post)\(/ matching Deno.env.get and c.get; Git Bash mangling /api/... arguments into Windows paths; a middleware named apiKeyAuthMiddleware not matching a pattern written as apiKeyMiddleware). A guard built on that modelling would cry wolf on every new public endpoint and get suppressed, which is worse than no guard. Converting the allowlist to per-namespace wildcards plus explicit public opt-outs would be the real fix, and that is a deliberate refactor rather than a check.

userStories.title: Accessibility audit of all 214 prerendered pages — two heading-level skips fixed, everything else clean
userStories.notes:
Audited the shipped HTML for accessibility signals with an unambiguous ground truth (no contrast maths, no judgement about 'meaningful' text). CLEAN across 214 pages, which is a real result and not a null one: every has an alt attribute, every page has , every page has exactly one

, no anchor lacks an accessible name, and there is no positive tabindex anywhere. FIXED — two heading-level skips: - /tools/fit-checker: h1 -> h3 for the two form-section headings ('The garment', 'Your body'), which then sat ABOVE the page's h2 sections. Now h2. - / (landing): h2 -> h4 on the 'Included with FlipDesk' card. Now h3. Both were caused by the same thing: the tag was chosen for its font size (an h3 for text-sm, an h4 for a card) rather than for its position in the outline. That is invisible in review because the page LOOKS correct — the damage is only to anyone navigating by heading, who is told a nesting level exists that does not, so a section appears nested under a parent that was never announced. Most screen-reader users navigate by heading rather than reading linearly, so this is the structure they rely on. TWO FALSE POSITIVES from my own audit, verified and dismissed rather than filed: the hidden file inputs on /tools/grade-checker and /tools/authenticity-check are flagged as 'input with no accessible name', but class="hidden" is Tailwind display:none, which removes the element from the accessibility tree entirely. A visually-hidden input triggered by a labelled button is the standard accessible upload pattern, not a defect. Guard: src/prerender/__tests__/heading-outline.test.ts asserts exactly one h1 and no skipped level across every prerendered page, plus a floor of 200 pages so a partial dist cannot make it pass trivially. It runs against the SHIPPED HTML rather than components, because the level a heading lands on depends on the layout wrapping it — something no component-level test can see. Sabotage-verified by reverting the landing h3 to h4.

userStories.title: prd-lint blocked two agents at once: planning fields on finished records, and a string nextId
userStories.description: As either agent writing to prd.json, I want the linter to encode the invariants that matter rather than a single agent's house style, so that a legitimate convention from one workflow does not turn CI red for everyone.
acceptanceCriteria: DONE: description and acceptanceCriteria are now required only on passes:false stories. They are PLANNING fields — a finished record cannot be planned, and requiring them rejected a legitimate use that emerged in practice (recording a completed audit or a negative result as {id, title, passes, notes}). They remain required on the actionable backlog, which is the only place they do work and the only thing the Ralph loop selects from.

DONE: nextId accepts 2088 or "US-2088". Only prd-lint reads it, so the form is style; the invariant that it must beat every id anywhere is what matters, and that is enforced for both. The string form is canonical because it is what an author copies straight into a new id.

DONE: fixed two real data errors the relaxed rules then exposed — a story with id "2077" missing its US- prefix (invisible to parseIdNum, so it did not count toward maxActive), and US-2078 sitting in the ACTIVE backlog with no description or acceptance criteria.

US-2078 planning fields were DERIVED from that story's own "REMAINING (this story)" note rather than invented, and the first AC says so, so the owning agent can re-scope without having to guess what was assumed.
DONE: 9 tests across both rules, each in both directions.
userStories.notes: [P1][Tooling][Agents] Filed and fixed 2026-07-19 while two agents were writing prd.json concurrently. prd-lint had been red on main: the other agent uses record-shaped stories for completed audits and a string nextId; both are reasonable, both failed the linter. Resolved by relaxing the linter to the invariants rather than making either agent conform — the alternative was rewriting another agent's live convention mid-flight. The relaxation is narrow: unfinished stories still need planning fields, so the guard still catches an unplannable story entering the queue.

userStories.title: Newsletter kickoff cron has returned HTTP 500 hourly since 2026-07-01 — a discarded auth response left the Hono context unfinalized
userStories.notes:
Found by querying Sentry for real production errors rather than reading code. GRADETHREAD-FRONTEND-T: 'Context is not finalized. You may forget returning Response object or `await next()`', thrown from hono-base.ts:358, culprit POST /api/newsletter/scheduler/tick. 168 occurrences, hourly, first seen 2026-07-01, still firing at 03:00 today. Source IP is the scheduled-task caller.

ROOT CAUSE: schedulerAuth's JWT fallback ran the auth middlewares but discarded their return value:
    await authMiddleware(c, async () => { await adminAuthMiddleware(c, next) })
    // middleware ends -> returns undefined
Hono finalizes a context from the middleware's RETURN VALUE. authMiddleware built its 401, the wrapper dropped it, nothing finalized, Hono threw, and onError converted it into a 500. So a clean 401 was being served as a 500 — and because the framework error carries NO STACK, the real trigger stayed invisible.

WHAT THE 401 MEANS — the part that matters commercially: the fallback only runs when the job secret does NOT verify. The newsletter kickoff cron has therefore been rejected on every run since 2026-07-01. No issue creation, no advance, no dispatch for 18 days. The bug did not break the newsletter; it HID that the newsletter was already broken, by turning an actionable 401 (rotate/set NEWSLETTER_INTERNAL_JOB_SECRET) into an opaque framework 500.

SCOPE: the same wrapper is copy-pasted in content-scheduler.ts and drip.ts — the comment in newsletter-scheduler.ts even says it 'mirrors' them. All three fixed. Only the newsletter one is firing in Sentry, which suggests the other two secrets still verify, so their identical bug is latent rather than active.

FIX: capture and propagate the rejection (Hono's Next type is () => Promise<void>, so the inner response cannot simply be returned). adminAuthMiddleware's 403 wins when present, else authMiddleware's 401, else undefined so the handler finalizes normally.

GUARDS (scheduler-auth-finalizes_test.ts), both sabotage-verified:
  1. Source guard — none of the three files may discard the auth response, and each must still call authMiddleware (so a rename fails loudly instead of passing over a file it no longer understands).
  2. Behavioural guard — builds a Hono app with the OLD shape and asserts it yields 500, and with the FIXED shape and asserts 401. This pins the framework behaviour the fix depends on, so a Hono upgrade that changed it fails here rather than silently reintroducing 500s.

⚠️ REQUIRES AN EDGE REDEPLOY (Coolify) — this is edge code, not auto-deployed by the Pages push. AND the underlying secret still needs fixing: after deploy the endpoint will return a clean 401 instead of a 500, but the newsletter still will not run until NEWSLETTER_INTERNAL_JOB_SECRET (or _OLD, for rotation overlap) matches what the scheduled task sends.

userStories.title: Invalid certificate URLs returned 503 Retry-After to crawlers instead of 404 — unvalidated UUIDs reached Postgres
userStories.notes:
Second finding from the Sentry queue. Five separate open issues, all one root cause: GET /api/content/public/certificates/<junk> passed the path param straight into .eq("certificate_id", …) on a uuid COLUMN, so Postgres raised 22P02 ("invalid input syntax for type uuid") and publicError() reported it as a 500 plus a Sentry capture. Because the junk value is in the error message, every distinct probe created a NEW Sentry issue — EXAMPLE, not-a-uuid-xyz, %3Cid%3E, <id>&quot, abcdef01-2345-6789 — so ordinary scanner traffic was steadily polluting the error dashboard and could bury a real error.

THE ACTUAL DAMAGE was downstream and worse than noise. functions/cert/[id].ts treats any non-404 upstream reply as UpstreamUnavailable and answers 503 + Retry-After. That behaviour is correct and deliberate (US-2044, so a transient blip is never reported to a crawler as 'gone') — but it amplified this bug: a 500 for a permanently invalid id became a 503 telling search engines to retry a URL that can never exist. VERIFIED LIVE before the fix: https://gradethread.com/cert/EXAMPLE and /cert/not-a-uuid-xyz both returned 503.

Notable: this is my own earlier work interacting badly with a pre-existing bug. US-2044 made the SSR layer strictly honest about the difference between 'absent' and 'unreachable'. That was right, and it converted an upstream 500 into a louder, more harmful signal. Worth remembering that hardening one layer can raise the cost of a defect in another.

FIX: an isUuid() guard applied to all three certificate-UUID routes (/certificates/:id, /cert-image/:id, /certificates/:id/verify) BEFORE any query. A malformed id cannot match a row, so 404 is the honest answer — and is what those routes' own comments already promised.

GUARDS (cert-id-validation_test.ts), sabotage-verified by removing the check from /cert-image/:id:
  1. Each of the three routes must call isUuid(), and must do so BEFORE its first supabase call — validating after the query starts would still let the bad value reach the database.
  2. The pattern is exercised against real UUIDs (accepted) and against every junk value that actually produced a Sentry issue in production (rejected), plus a truncated UUID and an unhyphenated one.

⚠️ REQUIRES AN EDGE REDEPLOY (Coolify) to take effect, same as US-2087. After deploy, /cert/<junk> should return the branded 404 page rather than 503 — worth re-checking the two URLs above to confirm.
